stories.body:
Bosses of Citroën owner and French carmaker also urge UK government to consider limiting imports from China

Stellantis and Renault have backed the UK car industry for inclusion in proposed rules to protect EU industry, but urged the British government to consider limiting imports of Chinese cars.

Emanuele Cappellano, who leads Stellantis’s European brands including Fiat, Citroën, Opel and Vauxhall, and François Provost, the chief executive of France’s Renault, said the UK should effectively be counted as one of the EU’s 27 member states for the purposes of the proposed “Made in Europe” legislation .

The new rules aim to ensure EU subsidies and government procurement benefits Europe’s industry, rather than helping manufacturers from other countries.

The executives were speaking at the Paris motor show, which was attended on Monday by the French president, Emmanuel Macron. Brands including Li Auto, GAC and Chery were among a host of Chinese manufacturers exhibiting in Paris with ambitious European expansion plans.

Europe’s car industry is under enormous pressure as it copes with lower demand than before the coronavirus pandemic, while also investing tens of billions of euros in shifting production to electric vehicles (EVs). At the same time, Chinese carmakers’ market share has soared as the transition to EVs opens the door to new entrants.

The EU confirmed on Monday it would limit the number of hybrid electric vehicles imported from China to 350,000 cars a year. The EU expects that the quota, which will come into force in December, will halve China’s market share, which now stands at 6% in a landmark four-year agreement made in Beijing last week.

The Made in Europe rules are another plank of the EU’s response to the rise of China in key manufacturing industries such as carmaking and chemicals.

Under the proposed Industrial Accelerator Act (IAA), cars will have to be “made in Europe”, and contain enough European parts and materials, to continue to qualify for EV grants and to be bought by public bodies in the EU. However, automotive manufacturers and politicians are haggling over the details.

If Brussels sticks to a strict definition of “European” as being only EU countries, Britain risks being left out – prompting intense lobbying from UK car industry and government to be included.

Stellantis is among the manufacturers that still has a British factory, its facility in Ellesmere Port, Merseyside, which produces small vans.

“I think that UK somehow needs to be equalised to the EU 27,” said Cappellano, referring to the bloc’s 27 member states. “We have a lot of relationship, we have footprint. Historically UK has been very close to the European market.”

Europe’s main automotive lobby groups ACEA and Clepa have also put their weight behind the UK to be included. Some parts of European manufacturing, including France’s industry minister , had argued that the UK should be left out given Brexit.

Provost said there was “no other choice” but a deal between the UK and EU. However, he said the UK would also have to stop allowing Chinese cars in without limits.

“On your side, you have also to take decisions,” he said. “If the UK is willing to join the European ecosystem, this is to have an industrial ambition … to keep a strong automotive industry.”

after newsletter promotion

He said this would be an industry that “is not closed to Chinese competitors, but … if you want to operate in Europe, you have to deeply invest in the whole value chain, final manufacturing, suppliers, R&D, technologies.”

Provost added: “I’m not here to demand whatsoever, but I think if UK is willing to join this ecosystem of IAA, there is some open question about the level of imports.”

London has so far rejected pressure to impose its own tariffs on Chinese imports, but the UK business secretary, Jonathan Reynolds, this month said that decision was under review .

Cappellano also said the UK should consider imposing tariffs on Chinese imports. “It’s very important that the UK defines what is the priority,” he said. “It’s very difficult to defend industrial footprint and at the same time let the market completely open to import. Either one or the other.”

He expressed scepticism over whether other countries beyond the EU such as Japan, Turkey and Morocco should be included in the rules.

“We don’t necessarily need to have a larger definition of European scope,” he said, pointing to proposals that carmakers be allowed to source 30% of their materials from outside the EU.

He also argued for more time until 2030 for manufacturers to source batteries from within Europe. China is dominant in the global supply of batteries and Cappellano said it would take longer to build up the European industry.

stories.title: Long-lost horror gaming cult classic P.T. gets a much-needed PC port
stories.summary: Kojima's discontinued "playable trailer" is no longer stuck on a few aging PS4 hard drives.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Kojima’s discontinued “playable trailer” is no longer stuck on a few aging PS4 hard drives.

For over a decade now, the only “official” way to play Hideo Kojima’s cult classic, P.T. —the long-discontinued “playable trailer” for Kojima’s canceled “Silent Hills” project —has been via one of the increasingly rare PlayStation 4s that previously downloaded a copy during its monthslong availability window. Now, though, one coder is helping to preserve the game with a porting tool that builds a playable x86 PC executable from the original PS4 files.

Coder Lorean Xavier said he was inspired to work on the “P.T. for PC” project “because P.T. deserved to keep existing somewhere other than on consoles that still have it installed.” The open source porting effort rebuilds the P.T. engine in C++ and Vulkan, using the original files from the PS4 game to re-create “every level, model, texture, sound, script and cutscene,” according to its GitHub listing. That means players without their own legitimate decrypted copy of the original P.T. will have to track one down in order to generate a playable PC version.

The reliance on real P.T. files makes this port more authentic than previous hobbyist efforts to re-create the look and feel of P.T. for a PC audience. And while PS4 emulators recently reached a point where they could run P.T. completely , this native port also sports extra features, like upscaling and frame-generation, a camera mode, experimental third-person and VR support, and a “museum” section where you can look at and listen to in-game assets (including “unused content”).

Although Xavier admits to using AI tools in developing this port, it doesn’t seem like he simply followed the recent retro-gaming trend of asking a coding agent to decompile the game. On social media , Xavier said that he has “spent years studying P.T. and Fox Engine” in developing the port and only uses AI tools “for debugging, troubleshooting and investigating problems.”

“I’m a solo developer making a free P.T. port because I love the game,” he added. “Nobody hired me or asked me to spend countless hours on this. I’m sharing something I worked incredibly hard on, simply because I want other people to enjoy it.”

Beyond being of interest to curious gamers who never had access to the extremely limited PS4 version, this port of P.T. should be very useful to preservationists who want to maintain public access to this historically significant game for generations going forward. “Personally… I think the hardware super-specific solutions are dead ends for preservation,” Henry Lowood, curator for the History of Science & Technology Collections and Film & Media Collections in the Stanford University Libraries, told Ars back in 2015 . “The kinds of equipment/hardware we have, the way they’re manufactured, just have a very small likelihood of surviving for super long periods of time.”

stories.title: Trump faces growing backlash over plans to import diesel from Russia
stories.summary: Both Republican and Democratic lawmakers have criticised the deal, which was announced weeks before the US midterm elections.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Global fuel prices have soared since the US-Israel war with Iran began at the end of February

Published 12 October 2026, 00:18 BST

US President Donald Trump is facing a growing backlash over plans to import diesel from Russia as the Iran war continues to impact global energy prices.

Trump on Friday announced that Russian President Vladimir Putin had agreed to release 300,000 tonnes of diesel immediately "to the American and global marketplace" followed by several other shipments.

That is despite signing legislation to authorise fresh US sanctions and tariffs on nations that import Russian oil and gas just weeks ago.

The move has been criticised by some Republican and Democratic lawmakers, who believe the deal violates US laws.

As well as the initial release of 300,000 tonnes of diesel, Trump said Russia would then supply 500,000 tonnes in November and one million more after that.

This would be followed by a further three million tonnes, which would be delivered "within a short period" dependent on the condition of its refineries, which have been attacked by Ukraine during the ongoing war between the two countries.

"Lower prices for Americans, especially our Great Farmers, Ranchers, and Truckers, is my Greatest Priority," Trump wrote in a Truth Social post.

Russia's Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak confirmed these numbers to Tass, the country's state-owned news agency, saying the export volume could reach three million tonnes per month in future.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has called the deal a gift to Putin that amounts to "an investment in a war that must be ended".

It is understood the US Treasury is suspending sanctions on Russian diesel exports until 7 April as part of the deal, but other assets like those in American banks are still frozen.

A group of seven senators - four Republicans and three Democrats – on Sunday said the deal violated US laws, urging Trump to "reverse course".

"The United States should not provide Putin with a financial lifeline while Russia continues to kill Ukrainian civilians," the lawmakers said.

They added that Congress had "explicitly banned Russian energy imports in 2022 to prevent American dollars from financing Putin's brutal war against Ukraine".

The statement was signed by Republicans Susan Collins, Lisa Murkowski, Thom Tillis and John Curtis, as well as Democrats Jeanne Shaheen, Richard Blumenthal and Ron Wyden.

Trump wants to reduce the cost of fuel as the midterms loom - will it work? Published 2 days ago

Analysis: Trump's shock Russia deal highlights mounting pressure to curb fuel prices Published 2 days ago

Not everyone is opposed to the deal. Republican Thomas Massie, who has sparred with Trump a number of issues, said the US should lift sanctions on all petroleum products.

Trump's Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told Fox News the agreement would work through existing legal channels the US has to help bring prices down and that anyone in Congress who said it would not was wrong.

Global fuel prices have soared since the US-Israel war with Iran began at the end of February, with the fighting severely disrupting supplies of crude oil - a key ingredient in petrol and diesel.

The rising prices have become a key issue for Americans ahead of next month's midterms elections, which will determine if Trump's Republican Party maintains control of Congress.

Polls show a majority of Americans disapprove of his handling of the economy and the war in Iran and he has been searching for ways to ease his party's political pain.

The toll the war is taking has been acutely felt by US agricultural states, which rely heavily on diesel to operate farming machinery and to transport their products to market.

The average diesel price in the US is currently $6.28 (£4.74) a gallon, according to the AAA, down from the record high of $6.53 recorded at the end of September.

Analysts have questioned whether Russia is capable of providing that quantity of diesel and the extent to which doing so will ease prices for American consumers.

The US uses approximately 3.6 million barrels of diesel a day, so even if Russia delivers its promised 300,000 tonnes this month, it amounts to approximately half of the US daily consumption.

It is not only at home that Trump is facing opposition to his diesel deal with Russia. A number of international leaders have criticised it, including Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney and UK Defence Secretary Wes Streeting, who said the US and other allies of Ukraine should focus on ramping up pressure on Russia to end the war.

Meanwhile, Trump announced in Sunday that Russia and Ukraine had reached an "energy ceasefire" but did not give more details. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky welcomed this but there was no response from Moscow.

stories.body:
Brussels uses WTO rules to quickly impose quota, which will halve Chinese market share to 3%

Business live – latest updates

VW boss backs EU plan to bolster domestic industry

The EU is to limit the number of hybrid electric vehicles imported from China to 350,000 cars a year, the European Commission has confirmed.

Imports have been soaring in the past two years; about 800,000 battery and plug-in hybrids are likely to be sold this year.

The EU expects that the quota, which will come into force in December, will halve China’s market share, which now stands at 6% in a landmark four-year agreement made in Beijing last week .

The annual limit on imports of hybrids will be taken under the World Trade Organization safeguard measures, which mean it can be implemented swiftly without the type of investigations needed in anti-dumping measures.

Any cars imported above the quota level will not be subject to tariffs, but will remain blocked in customs at docks in Europe.

Chinese vehicles assembled within the EU, such as those made in Hungary or, in future, Spain, will not be subject to the quota, officials have confirmed, but EU companies making cars in China will.

China’s exports of hybrids to the EU tripled to €6.7bn (£5.7bn) in the first half of this year, from €2.2bn a year earlier, according to Chinese customs data.

As part of the deal, China has also agreed to drop some tariffs on auto parts and cut duties by half on footwear, olive oil and ice-cream from the EU.

Officials stressed that the quota is fully supported by China, and further dialogue on cars and other imports including chemicals, renewable energy and furniture is continuing.

“We will continue the dialogue on some products … this is by no means the end of the story,” an official said.

Last month, the EU called for feedback on a new rule that could oblige companies to diversify their supply chains while the “Made in Europe” legislation would do the same in public procurement.

On Thursday, EU leaders will discuss a French-German proposal for a “kill switch” or new instrument that would allow Brussels to block access to the single market for certain goods in the event of any harmful development, such as a ban on rare earths crucial for the tech and automotive industries.

after newsletter promotion

The deal on hybrid EVs comes amid mounting concern over the £1bn-a-day trade deficit the EU is now running with China.

Up until recently, the EU’s strategy for tackling what it says is an “unsustainable” trade imbalance has been to seek to increase exports to China.

Sources said there has been “a paradigm shift” with concerns of deindustrialisation and job losses in the industrial heartlands forcing a renewed focus on curbing imports rather than increasing exports.

“We are closely surveilling, our imports. We know what’s coming in. We know where there’s a surge, and we know what hits the hardest in terms of our deindustrialisation,” said an official.

Andrew Small, the director of the Asia programme at the European Council for Foreign Relations, said China was likely to “suck the EU into drawn-out negotiations” on other sectors but the mood had changed in the EU.

“I think if China had offered a deal like this earlier in the year, say in spring, it would have been much easier to take the heat out. My sense is that things have now moved somewhat too far politically,” he said.

stories.title: Motion of no-confidence in Sinn Féin ministers 'pointless' - O'Neill
stories.summary: The motion against Michelle O'Neill and three other Sinn Féin ministers will be debated after receiving the backing of unionist parties last week.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
The motions against Michelle O'Neill (centre), Liz Kimmins (left), John O'Dowd and Caoimhe Archibald (right) are being debated after receiving the backing of unionist parties last week

Published 12 October 2026, 09:35 BST

The First Minister Michelle O'Neill has dismissed as "pointless" motions of no-confidence in her and three other Sinn Féin ministers.

The Northern Ireland Assembly has started debating the no-confidence motions over the ministers' handling of the Drumcree dispute, after they received the backing of unionist parties last week .

However, the attempt to oust them will fail as it requires cross-community support from a majority of both unionists and nationalists in the assembly.

It comes amid a major political row over a planned Orange Order march in Portadown, County Armagh.

What is the Garvaghy Road dispute all about?

O'Neill and other senior Sinn Féin politicians have been heavily criticised by unionists for joining protests which have blocked the parade from passing along the mainly nationalist Garvaghy Road.

Police are investigating the demonstrations in a "large-scale" criminal inquiry .

The first minister again defended her involvement in blocking the Garvaghy Road during the debate, describing the planned Orange Order march as "triumphalist and sectarian".

Motions of no-confidence in the assembly are not binding without cross-community support from both unionist and nationalist MLAs, and cannot automatically force a minister from office.

'First minister of lawlessness'

Speaking in the assembly, Traditional Unionist Voice (TUV) member Timothy Gaston, who tabled the no-confidence motions, described O'Neill as the "first minister of lawlessness" who "doesn't want an Orangeman about the place".

He asked: "If a determination can be set aside simply because republican protesters object to it, what confidence can any loyalist, any Orangeman, any unionist, have in the impartial administration of justice here in Northern Ireland?"

He said there needed to be "political consequences" for Sinn Féin and reiterated TUV's call for the Democratic Unionist Party (DUP) to withdraw their deputy first minister to trigger the removal of O'Neill from the first minister post.

Michelle O'Neill has defended her actions, saying she was "proud" to stand with the residents

O'Neill said it was "no surprise" unionist parties had supported the no-confidence motions because "they have never accepted equality".

"They have never accepted rights and respect, and again they still haven't respected the fact that it is now 2026."

The exclusion motions have also been submitted against John O'Dowd, Caoimhe Archibald and Liz Kimmins.

O'Dowd, who is also the finance minister, told the assembly he was "proud" to stand with the Garvaghy Road residents.

He accused the TUV of wanting to bring Stormont down.

Earlier, he told BBC Radio Ulster's Good Morning Ulster programme that he would continue to work with other parties.

"I am seeking engagements around the budget, I want to work with parties to make a better society for everyone."

Economy Minister Caoimhe Archibald said the parading dispute had been used to create "instability" and said "the days of Orange domination are done".

Kimmins, who is the infrastructure minister, added that she had seen both "some of the most regressive elements of loyalism and unionism" over recent weeks and "the very best of our communities" in support of Garvaghy Road residents.

TUV assembly member Timothy Gaston (right) alongside party leader Jim Allister

The motions gained the required 30 signatures with the backing of assembly members from the Democratic Unionist Party (DUP) and the Ulster Unionist Party (UUP).

Speaking to BBC Radio Ulster's Good Morning Ulster programme , the TUV leader, Jim Allister, admitted the debate was "not going to succeed succeed because of the absurd system whereby it needs cross-community support".

"But that accentuates the pressure on the DUP to be seen to do something because as things stand lawbreakers are sitting in our executive."

'Abject failure'

DUP assembly member Jonathan Buckley, who signed the no-confidence motions, accused Sinn Féin of "abject failure of political leadership".

"The genesis of today's debate may be about a parade, but it is about much more," he told the assembly.

"It is about the rule of law. It is about those who feel they are above it and not accountable to it".

Earlier, DUP leader Gavin Robinson called for sanctions to be introduced against anyone who broke the law.

Robinson said he plans to speak to the secretary of state on Monday evening to ensure that there is "accountability".

He said the legislation should be "brought forward that will bring sanctions so that anyone who has broken the law is subject to it and punished".

Regarding what actions the DUP could take, Robinson said "nothing is of the table".

DUP leader Gavin Robinson said that removing Emma Little-Pengelly as deputy first minister would "punish everybody else"

The DUP and Ulster Unionists share power with Sinn Féin in a four-party devolved government alongside the Alliance Party.

Jim Allister has been urging the DUP to withdraw Emma Little-Pengelly as deputy first minister to trigger the removal of O'Neill as first minister.

Earlier on Good Morning Ulster , Robinson had said that he is "not in the territory" to "destabilise".

However his party colleague, Carla Lockhart, who represents the Upper Bann constituency in Westminster, said it "cannot be business as usual" at Stormont and the DUP has it "within its gift to remove" O'Neill from her position.

Robinson said that when the party comes to a "consensus, that is our position".

He added that Lockhart has "the right to stand up for her constituents".

DUP MP Carla Lockhart said it "cannot be business as usual" at Stormont

Alliance Party deputy leader Eóin Tennyson branded the no-confidence motions a "political stunt" designed to collapse Stormont.

Tennyson described the debate as "depressing, dispiriting and almost unbelievable", warning that power-sharing institutions were "once again being placed in jeopardy".

However, he also said any elected representatives found to have acted unlawfully in recent weeks "should face the consequences of that conduct".

Ahead of the debate at Stormont, the leader of the opposition, the SDLP's Matthew O'Toole, said politicians were entitled to express their views but needed to move forward once proceedings had concluded.

O'Toole said attention should then return to issues affecting people across Northern Ireland, adding: "If they work in the public sector, they might be waiting on a pay rise. They might have a family member stuck on a waiting list."

UUP leader Jon Burrows said withdrawing ministers from the executive is not the answer.

Speaking on BBC Radio Ulster's Nolan Show, he said: "I will not remove Robbie Butler at this late stage, because to do so would affect the people of Northern Ireland in all the work he is doing."

Burrows said he was instead calling for changes to Stormont's rules, and said there should be "proper accountability mechanisms" to hold ministers who breach the pledge of office to account.

stories.title: F1 in Singapore: There's a new fastest car now
stories.summary: Also, F1’s final sprint saw our first real wet racing of the year.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.imageAlt: SINGAPORE, SINGAPORE - OCTOBER 10: Marshals sweep away the standing water on track as the rain falls prior to the Sprint ahead of the F1 Grand Prix of Singapore at Marina Bay Street Circuit on October 10, 2026 in Singapore, Singapore. (Photo by Mark Thompson/Getty Images)
stories.body:
Also, F1’s final sprint saw our first real wet racing of the year.

Formula 1’s lengthy 2026 season is entering its final stretch. The sport took to the floodlit streets of Singapore on Sunday night, but Saturday saw action, too; this Grand Prix weekend was also the final of six sprints this year. The night race might be one of modern F1’s greatest spectacles. From overhead shots, the track becomes a bright, illuminated ribbon among the looming darkness of the city-state’s overpasses and skyscrapers. At ground level, the cars shower glittering sparks from their titanium skid blocks as the drivers flirt with how close they can get to the walls. As tracks go, the 90-degree turns and concrete barrier-lined streets were a world away from the abrasive tarmac and ample runoff of Malaysia last time out . But the tropical heat and humidity were a constant given both locations’ proximity to the equator.

Showers for the sprint

In Malaysia (which was still technically the Bahrain GP), a pre-race downpour disrupted things mightily. On Saturday morning in Singapore, shortly before the start of the sprint, it seemed history was about to rhyme when the skies opened. With standing water in places on the track, the sprint was delayed by 30 minutes. The sprint format, where a short extra race replaces a practice session a day before the main event, is unloved by the drivers and teams. For one thing, there’s little prestige in winning Saturday’s sprint. And with qualifying just a few hours later, risk-taking is discouraged lest one wreck the car and ruin Sunday’s race a day early.

And in Singapore, like most street circuits, the proximity of the unyielding barriers that line the track means there are real, punishing consequences for getting it even a little wrong.

Which is what happened to George Russell. The Mercedes driver went into this season as the title favorite, only to see those hopes evaporated by a combination of car unreliability and a young teammate, Kimi Antonelli, who appears to be a generational talent. A win in Azerbaijan in September was a chance for Russell to get back on terms with Antonelli, but he failed to finish in Malaysia, and his sprint didn’t last much longer.

It started well. The track was still far too wet for slick tires, so the entire field lined up on intermediate treaded tires. Russell’s Mercedes made a much better start from second on the grid than polesitter Max Verstappen’s Red Bull, and he stole the lead. A lap later, Russell’s sprint was over, and his car bent and broken after he misjudged the final corner. On a wet race track, any painted sections become very slippery, something that goes double for street circuits. “I went a little bit wide, and then I touched the white line. The No. 1 rule in the rain is don’t touch the white line. It’s a very silly mistake–overly confident. I think it’s my first crash of the year. It’s annoying to happen from that position,” Russell said after the fact.

Cross that one off the list finally

Verstappen benefited from Russell’s mistake, inheriting the lead. For a while, Lewis Hamilton’s Ferrari appeared to be a threat. But intermediate tires will begin to overheat as the track dries, which soon affected Hamilton and the other Ferrari driver, Charles Leclerc. At the end of 20 laps, he crossed the finish line first. Surprisingly, this was Verstappen’s first victory in Singapore. Although, as mentioned, he didn’t exactly see it as such.

“I want to win tomorrow,” Verstappen said after the race. “I don’t see this as a win in terms of actually winning a Grand Prix, you know. So we need to have a good qualifying. It will be very close with a lot of cars, I think, and we just need to try and make sure, of course, we are the best one out of them. But it will be, yeah, hopefully a good battle.”

His Red Bull was recently updated, and in combination with a power unit that has the strongest V6 in the field (if perhaps not the best hybrid system), it may be the fastest car on the grid, at least in Verstappen’s capable hands. A few hours later, he secured pole position in qualifying for Sunday’s race. Like the sprint finishing order, he would have the two Ferraris behind him, albeit with Leclerc ahead of Hamilton.

It was a lights-to-flag victory for Verstappen, even with the added complication of radio troubles—he could hear his engineer, but his replies were unintelligible. Such was his pace and tire management that he was able to stop for tires and leave the pits without giving up the lead. “The car was really good on the tires. I could really manage them well. But to be honest, I think it was one of the first times that I’ve driven in clean air here in Singapore in the race, so I guess that’s also nice. And yeah, it’s been just a fantastic weekend for us,” Verstappen said.

The last three races have seen two wins and a second for Verstappen. “I really think, of course, that our car has taken a really nice step forward. But at the end of the day, yeah, it’s just been more driveable and more predictable. That’s what I wanted and needed from the car to find that last step to fight up front,” he said.

A newly resurgent Verstappen, currently in fourth place, could be a threat for second place in the standings by season’s end. Not that he really cares. “I hope that we can carry that momentum forward. We don’t really have anything to win in the championship, right? I think Kimi is miles ahead. For me, personally, I don’t care if I’m second, third, or fourth. Like, yeah, it doesn’t do anything. But I just want to have fun till the end, you know, try to go for a day’s success,” he said.

With both sprint and race poles, and sprint and race victories, it was almost a perfect weekend for Verstappen, who only missed out on the fastest lap to Leclerc, who came home second. It should have been a double podium for Ferrari. Hamilton did not have as much speed as Leclerc and started the race on an alternate strategy, using the medium tires instead of the softs.

These didn’t last long though, and Hamilton stopped on lap 17, switching to the softs. With most of the 62-lap race left to run, that set up the potential for a very long afternoon. And when Lance Stroll’s Aston Martin broke down as usual and caused a virtual safety car period, inexplicably Hamilton overrode the team’s instructions to follow Leclerc into the pits to solve the problem by making a cheap stop. Staying out on increasingly ruined tires left the seven-time champion a sitting duck to cars behind, and he turned third into sixth, apologizing to his team on the radio afterward.

More teammate fights

As we have discussed more than once this season, perhaps the cardinal rule as an F1 driver is “don’t hit your teammate.” That we’ve seen teammates battling a lot isn’t entirely unsurprising—if the cars are stratified by pace, and a team has two drivers of about the same caliber, then if they both perform well, they should qualify in similar positions and therefore find themselves racing together. Haas’ Oliver Bearman showed the right way to do that, going side by side with his teammate Esteban Ocon for several corners on lap 3, a battle that was sadly relegated to a small Picture in Picture window on the broadcast. (A couple of laps later, Bearman followed it with a late move on Carlos Sainz’ Williams, too.)

Sometimes, we see situations like Ferrari has faced in recent races, including this one, splitting strategies between two cars but with the car on newer, faster tires stuck behind the car on older, slower rubber. Sometimes the driver in front does what’s best for the team and lets them by without a fight—Hamilton did just this late in the race when a much faster Leclerc on much newer tires needed to get by.

What no fan—or team boss—wants to see is both their cars trying to take the same piece of tarmac. Which is exactly what happened with McLaren’s pair during Saturday’s sprint. The orange cars were in fourth (Piastri) and fifth (Norris) on the last lap of the race when Norris decided to try to invert that order. The pair made contact, Piastri’s car broke, and Norris finished eighth. Nine points for the team turned into one point, and Norris had given the team extra work to do to repair the other car in time for qualifying.

McLaren’s team principal, Andrea Stella, called the incident “unacceptable” and presumably read the riot act to his driver. Norris was suitably chastened the following day, both offering to help Piastri in the race if he could, and telling journalists after the race that “I can’t attempt what I did. I should never have attempted it in the first place, even if the move was on. I’ve simply got to think more of the team that I represent rather than myself. It was a mistake on my part, and I let down the team,” Norris said.

A title in Texas

With this Asian leg complete, the F1 circus now relocates to the Americas, starting with the Circuit of the Americas in Austin, Texas. There’s a chance Antonelli could clinch the title if he leaves Texas 125 points ahead of his closest rival. Currently, that’s George Russell, who trails by 102 points, with Hamilton in third at 111 points behind, and Verstappen 119 points behind Antonelli in fourth.

A win is worth 25 points, so it’s possible, but it would require yet more bad luck from Russell; by my admittedly terrible arithmetic, if Russell finishes ninth and only scores two points to an Antonelli win, his title hopes are over. But if he finishes eighth and scores four points, or does better, his hopes stay alive at least until the following round in Mexico.

Similar elimination calculations exist to rule out Hamilton and Verstappen, with higher finishing positions required to stay in it due to their greater points deficits to the leader. Given Verstappen’s form recently, and Mercedes’ inability to make its own upgrade work quite so well, there’s every prospect of a third consecutive Red Bull win in a couple of weeks. And Lewis Hamilton has finished on the podium at COTA nine times now, so he knows how to find a result there, even if a Ferrari victory seems unlikely.

Ars will be on the ground in Austin, where I’m hoping to learn more about how the teams program these fiendishly complicated power units and see who’s prepared to talk about those carbon-neutral synthetic fuels the sport was so keen to tell me about just a few short years ago .

stories.body:
Thinktank’s influential pre-budget report urges key decisions to be made now and not put off until next year

John Healey has been warned by Britain’s leading tax and spending experts that his budget risks being a “work of fiction” unless he sets out plans to cover £35bn in spending pressures.

As the war in the Middle East rattles the public finances, the Institute for Fiscal Studies (IFS) said the damage from higher inflation meant the chancellor would need to either top up funds for his current government spending plans or impose deep real-terms cuts by the end of the decade.

Against a febrile backdrop in the bond market, the thinktank warned Healey that failure to address the issue at his 28 October budget risked leaving the impression that Labour was setting unrealistic spending plans.

Helen Miller, the director of the IFS, said: “Simply pencilling in implicit cuts that he has no intention of delivering would make the budget a work of fiction.”

Her comment echoes a criticism levelled at Jeremy Hunt , the former Conservative chancellor, who before the 2024 general election was accused by the then head of the Office for Budget Responsibility of setting unrealistic spending plans.

Publishing its influential “green budget” report, which analyses the public finances before Healey’s speech to the Commons, it called on the chancellor to avoid announcing a “steady as she goes” budget that delayed decisions until next year’s spending review.

“If John Healey sets out spending envelopes for public services that he would not be willing to live within, his plan for meeting the fiscal rules will not be credible,” it said.

Last week, the governor of the Bank of England, Andrew Bailey, said fiscal policy “must be credible and be seen as such by financial markets”. The following day, the Times quoted a government source as saying: “Andrew Bailey needs to focus on doing his job.”

Miller said the Treasury adopting an assumption that “everything can be kicked forward” to next year’s spending review risked undermining the chancellor’s credibility.

“We would be better served by a chancellor who hopes for the best, but plans for the worst, rather than sets out plans that either say, ‘I hope it’ll be fine and some money will come in’, or ‘I’ll get a plan in a year’s time’.”

Attention before the budget has largely focused on the hit to the chancellor’s headroom against Labour’s main fiscal rule to balance day-to-day public spending with revenues in 2029-30.

With the war in the Middle East fuelling a dramatic sell-off in the market for government debt, higher borrowing costs are expected to erase a significant chunk of the £24bn buffer left by the former chancellor Rachel Reeves at the spring statement.

Leading economists have predicted the market moves since the start of the war in February could wipe out about half of the headroom, adding to nerves in the Treasury over the risk of a market backlash.

The IFS said that although the surge in debt interest costs could add £10bn to borrowing in 2029-30, the exchequer would benefit from higher inflation boosting tax revenue – meaning Healey could see headroom cut by only £4bn.

after newsletter promotion

However, it warned against focusing on this buffer because the inflation shock rippling from the Middle East would also dramatically hit the government’s plan for funding public services.

Higher inflation squeezes public spending power, forcing the government to choose between accepting real-term cuts and finding efficiency savings or topping up departmental budgets either by raising taxes or allowing an increase in borrowing.

The IFS said a choice to leave spending totals unchanged at the budget would implicitly mean allowing the quality or quantity of public services to fall. However, it said compensating for the inflation shock, and funding Healey’s pledge to raise defence spending to 3% of GDP by 2030, would require tax rises or benefit cuts of about £35bn.

“Choosing to stay the course with the inherited tax and spending plans would mean allowing inflation to blow departments’ spending plans off course,” Miller said.

“It would be a choice to tolerate chunky cuts to the quantity or quality of some public services – cuts that would be larger if defence spending was increased within existing totals.”

She said Healey would not need to make detailed plans for the next spending review period at the budget but merely set out overall spending envelopes that he would be prepared to live within.

A spokesperson for the Treasury said: “The chancellor is fully focused on his priorities to boost business, help with the cost of living and support people in every postcode, underpinned by fiscal discipline and a commitment to meet the fiscal rules with a buffer against uncertainty.

“The Office for Budget Responsibility will publish its updated forecast alongside the budget in October and we will not comment on rumour, speculation or proposals about its contents ahead of then.”

stories.title: Burnham to push for new post-Brexit deals at EU summit
stories.summary: Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch said the prime minister was "unpicking" the deal the UK signed with the EU.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Published 12 October 2026, 18:20 BST

Prime Minister Andy Burnham has told MPs that he will push for new post-Brexit deals with the EU at a summit next month.

He said "deeper cooperation" on some key issues - including youth mobility, food and drink, and energy - would help drive economic growth in the UK.

In a statement to MPs, Burnham also warned the EU's Made In Europe plans posed "a risk to UK manufacturing" and said he was in talks to get "an arrangement" that worked for the UK. The EU proposals aim to protect EU industry from Chinese competitors but could impact British industry and supply chains.

But Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch said the prime minister was "unpicking" the deal the UK signed with the EU.

Although he said he was keen to negotiate a closer relationship with the EU, Burnham also made clear Labour's manifesto commitments not to return to the single market, the customs union, or freedom of movement, would stay in place until the next election.

Burnham said that the "immediate priority" was securing a successful outcome at the November summit, adding: "I believe we should then set up a serious dialogue about the different options for our relationship in the long term.

"At every stage, the British public will be the boss, and I am clear that public opinion currently supports a pragmatic approach like the one I am suggesting."

While the prime minister has committed to the current Labour manifesto's red lines about Brexit, in interviews after Labour conference, he did not rule out a new manifesto, which could include re-joining the EU.

It is increasingly clear that economic growth, and cooperation on illegal immigration, are going to be at the centre of No 10's arguments when it comes to selling a closer relationship both at - and beyond - next month's summit.

There will be a series of deals with the EU on the table at the next summit, Burnham told MPs, including food and drink, energy trading, and coordinating on immigration.

Burnham claimed these agreements could add the equivalent of £10bn per year to the economy by 2040, arguing that it would be a "dereliction of duty" to turn away from the chance to cut bureaucracy.

"At present entire truckloads of plants or fresh produce can be destroyed because of a single missing stamp or a minor paperwork delay," he said.

"Fresh meat and fish spoil while waiting in trucks, and tonnes of exports have to be written off. Our largest food export, Scottish salmon, faces a 100% rate of document checks at the border, costing us around £100m in lost exports.

"British burgers and other fresh meat products cannot be sold in the EU, seed potatoes from Scotland and shellfish from Wales are banned - this is having a real impact on businesses and the agreement on the table could reverse some of that damage."

The Conservative leader criticised the prime minister for "unpicking the deal this country signed with the EU a decade after the referendum".

Badenoch added Burnham would not get a better deal than the one secured by the Conservatives, accusing him of giving the game away ahead of the summit.

"His exact words earlier this year were, 'the last thing we should do right now is re-run those arguments' and yet here he is unpicking the deal this country signed with the EU a decade after the referendum," she said.

"He is not going to get a better deal. The EU are tough negotiators, and it's not just that the EU are tough negotiators, he has already revealed his entire negotiating hand.

"He has just blurted out everything he wants in this statement and I will tell him now, as a former trade secretary, this is not how you conduct negotiations."

Mocking the previous negotiations, Burnham said: "She says that, oh, I've revealed what I want to do and this isn't any way to negotiate it - because the Tories were so good, weren't they, at negotiating deals with our partners?"

However, Liberal Democrat leader Sir Ed Davey welcomed Burnham's recognition of the "damage" of Brexit and called on him to go further, dropping Labour's red lines and opening negotiations on joining the EU single market and customs union.

stories.title: Germany news: Merz says Trump's Russia diesel deal 'out of question' for Europe
stories.summary: Chancellor Friedrich Merz has said that Donald Trump's diesel deal with Russia would be "out of the question" for Germany and the EU. Meanwhile, the ruling coalition has been rocked by a major resignation. DW has more.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Chancellor Friedrich Merz has said that Donald Trump's diesel deal with Russia would be "out of the question" for Germany and the EU. Meanwhile, the ruling coalition has been rocked by a major resignation. DW has more.

What you need to know

Merz said the order of the day was new EU sanctions on Russia not diesel deals with Russia, saying Ukraine's Volodymyr Zelenskyy 'can rely on Germany'

Bavarian state premier Markus Söder has accused some conservative bloc members in Saxony-Anhalt of being cowards

Bärbel Bas, Germany's education minister and the co-chair of the SPD, has resigned amid coalition infighting with Chancellor Merz's CDU

The winner of Germany's most prestigious literary peace prize has cricized the country's support of the Israeli government

Here are the latest headlines and reports from across Germany on Monday, October 12:

Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add DW as a Preferred Source on Google.

Police probe misuse of robot to sexually harass teenage girl

Police in Cologne say they are investigating the suspected use of a remote-controlled robot to sexually harass a 16-year-old girl over the weekend.

Police said the red and gold droid led to a police operation late on Saturday night on Cologne's ring road, allegedly as two young men were trying to get attention on social media.

"The gadget is alleged to have touched a 16-year-old [girl] on the posterior and to have bumped up against her rear end" more than once, police wrote.

"The 16-year-old [male] owner of the robot and his 19-year-old companion are suspected of filming the suspected assault, streaming it live online and providing commentary," police said.

The incident took place outside a fast food restaurant shortly before midnight.

Police arrived soon after and found robot inside the trunk or boot of a Volkswagen, saying that the 16-year-old owner had stowed it there prior to their arrival.

"How the robot was operating at the time of the crime and whether somebody was steering it with intent is now the subject of a criminal police investigation," police said, adding that they had seized both the robot and two of the suspects' phones.

New bridge opens at Danevirke Museum in Schleswig Holstein

German and Danish local politicians attended the ribbon cutting on Monday for a new pedestrian bridge near the town of Schleswig at the UNESCO heritage site the archaeological border complex of Hedeby and Danevirke (or Haithabu und Danewerk).

The new steel bridge links the walking path along the 11th century defenses of Danish King Valdemar's Wall with an artillery firing position engineered for Danish troops in the German-Danish war of 1864.

Valdemar's Wall was one of the earliest and largest secular brickwork structures of its time, built to defend the Danish kingdom from raids from Slavic and Saxon tribes.

Known as "Schanze 14" or "Entrenchment 14," the nearby elevated platform was built in 1864 to provide a good vantage point and natural terrain-based cover for Danish artillery fighting against Prussian troops in the Second Schleswig War.

Southern Schleswig, with a majority German population, forms part of the northermost state of Schlewsig-Holstein, while Northern Schleswig is in Denmark. The age-old disputes over the territory were largely settled in a 1955 treaty assuring minority rights on either side of the border.

German fighter jets to take part in NATO nuclear drill

Germany is sending three Tornado fighter jets to Italy to take part in NATO's annual nuclear deterrence exercise , Steadfast Noon, which begins on Tuesday.

The aircraft, normally stationed at Büchel air base in western Germany, have been deployed to Aviano Air Base in northern Italy, a German Air Force spokesperson told the DPA news agency.

Several dozen German military personnel will also participate in the exercise, which rehearses NATO's ability to deploy nuclear weapons in the event of a conflict.

No live nuclear weapons will be used. NATO says the exercise is routine, unrelated to current world events and not directed against any particular country.

The alliance has not disclosed details of this year's scenario. Last year's exercise involved around 2,000 personnel and more than 70 aircraft.

Germany participates in NATO's nuclear-sharing arrangements, under which German aircraft could deliver US nuclear weapons in a conflict.

Germany's Merz slams Trump's Russian diesel deal

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz has criticized US President Donald Trump's agreement to import Russian diesel, calling for tougher sanctions on Moscow instead.

"We take note of the agreement between the United States and Russia on diesel exports," Merz said in Berlin on Monday. "For Germany and Europe, such a decision is out of the question."

Merz said Russia would only negotiate seriously under pressure and called for further sanctions following Russian attacks on Ukraine's civilian energy infrastructure.

He also questioned Trump's announcement of an immediate halt to Russian and Ukrainian attacks on each other's energy facilities, saying Moscow had responded with massive strikes.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Trump's announcement of the partial ceasefire came as news to him, while the Kremlin has not confirmed that it has taken effect.

Merz reaffirmed Germany's support for Ukraine and said efforts to achieve a just and lasting peace would be discussed at this week's EU summit.

Can Ukraine still count on Germany?

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Tennis: Alexander Zverev will be world number 1 for the first time

The long-awaited mathematical confirmation has arrived: Germany's Alexander Zverez will take the top spot in the men's singles tennis rankings at the end of the year.

A shock straight set defeat for Carlos Alcaraz on Monday in Shanghai against unseeded Belgian player Zizou Bergs made Zverev claiming the number 1 ranking innevitable.

Aged 29, Zverev will be the oldest player ever to take over the top spot for the first time in his career.

He said that knowing he'd finish the season at number was a "dream come true," and said he'd concentrate on finishing the season "in style."

It's been a year of breakthroughs for Zverev, whose career to date had long seen him living in the shadows of greats like Roger Federer, Rafael Nadal and Novak Djokovic, and later Jannik Sinner and Carlos Alcaraz.

He won his first two Majors, at the French Open and then the US Open , and was also runner-up to Sinner at Wimbledon .

Sinner has not played since that final because of injury. Coupled with some patchy form from Alcaraz, this opened the door for Zverev to push to overtake them in the annual rankings.

The last — and only — German man to top tennis' world rankings was Boris Becker, who had two brief mid-season stints at number 1 in 1991. He did not finish the year as number 1, though.

Angelique Kerber also spent a combined seven and a half months at women's singles number 1 across three stints between 2016 and 2017, including at the end of the 2016 campaign. Steffi Graf meanwhile dominated the women's rankings for much of the period between 1987 and 1997.

SPD, Greens and Left party begin coalition talks in Mecklenburg-Lower Pomerania

The Social Democrats (SPD) have opened up coalition talks with the Greens and the Left party in Germany's northeastern state of Mecklenburg-Lower Pomerania, sources confirmed to local media.

The three parties have already held exploratory discussions on working together and received permission from party leadership bodies to move forward.

This comes several weeks after the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) came in first in the state election with 38.2% of the vote. However, without an outright majority and no other parties willing to work with them, they were unable to form a government.

Together the SPD, Greens and Left will hold 32 seats in the 71-member state parliament, giving them three more seats than the AfD.

The regional party leaders, including incumbent SPD state premier Manuela Schwesig , are expected to issue a joint statement later today.

The trio faces a tight turnaround to secure a coalition agreement, as the state's new parliament will sit for the first time on October 20, after which there is a four-week deadline to hold an election for premier.

Klingbeil cancels India trip, calls for SPD leadership vote

Vice-Chancellor and Finance Minister Lars Klingbeil has nixed a planned trip to India, saying that the Social Democrats need to hold a new vote for party leadership.

His announcement came shortly after the resignation of his party co-chair Bärbel Bas.

Klingbeil did not say whether he would run again, but confirmed that the rest of the party's top officials agreed the election was necessary.

Wadephul hails EU Russia sanctions

German Foreign Minsiter Johann Wadephul praised an "unprecedented sanctions blow" the European Union has levelled against Moscow.

"We are making it harder for Putin to continue his war of aggression in violation of international law, and his cynical attempt to wear down Ukraine's civilian population through murderous bombing campaigns," Wadephul said in a statement.

On Monday, EU foreign ministers met in Luxembourg to finalize the sanctions package.

It targets some 1,600 individuals and businesses related to Russia's war effort , and another 77 people and groups related to what the EU sees as illegal elections in occupied Ukrainian terrorities.

"We are increasing the pressure until Putin is ready to negotiate seriously about peace in Ukraine," Wadephul said, though he missed the Luxembourg meeting to participate in a CDU party summit in Berlin.

Frankfurt Book fair prize winner criticizes Germany's stance on Israel

Franco-British lawyer and author Philippe Sands accepted the prestigious Peace Price presented every year at the Frankfurt Book Fair, the premiere event of the German publishing industry.

Presdent Frank-Walter Steinmeier praised Sands as a committed humanist "who, despite growing resistance, fights tirelessly for human rights, justice and mutual understanding."

A professor of law at University College London and human rights lawyer at the International Court of Justice in The Hague, Sands used his acceptance speech to criticize Germany's "inappropiate silence" on the Israel's actions in the Gaza Strip and the occupied West Bank.

"It's not antisemitic. It's not anti-Israel. It's the truth," he said of the government's behavior.

You can read more about Sands and his speech here.

Cologne teenager badly injured while 'trainsurfing'

Public broadcaster WDR has said that 14-year-old was badly injured on Sunday night in Cologne after engaging in "trainsurfing," or attempting to ride on the top of a moving train.

The boy is reportedly fighting for his life at a local hospital after being struck by a powerful electrical current moving between the train and the overhead wires that power it. Authorities believe he could have been hit by 15,000 volts.

Trainsurfing is, of course, illegal, and still uncommon. However, authorities are worried that social media videos may encourage young people to attempt the dangerous stunt.

Söder: Those who voted for AfD speaker should show 'backbone'

"Do you want to go somewhere else? Then just say so," Bavarian leader Markus Söder said during an interview with public broadcaster ARD.

As a member of the CSU, the Bavarian sister party of Chancellor Merz's Christian Democrats (CDU), Söder was referencing bloc members in the state of Saxony-Anhalt who are believed to have voted for a member of the far-right in a secret ballot.

Last week, Tobias Rausch of the Alternative for Germany (AfD) — whose chapter in Saxony-Anhalt is classified as right-wing extremist — was elected state parliamentary speaker.

This marked the first time the AfD has seen a member elected to such a position, and the first time in postwar Germany that a right-wing extremist has risen to this rank.

AfD lawmaker elected speaker in Saxony-Anhalt

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The populist BSW party had declared their intention to support Rausch's nomination alongside the AfD, but his win with 48 votes means that other lawmakers must have voted for him too. It is strongly suspected that these were members of the conservative CDU.

Rausch's election prompted outrage across Germany, including from CDU members who have accused their colleagues of abandoning the so-called "firewall" — the agreement amongst the country's mainstream parties not to support the AfD.

Söder called it "pretty poor form," from the CDU members in Saxony-Anhalt, saying they should "at least have the backbone" to make their decision public.

Labor minister and SPD co-chair Bärbel Bas resigns

Citing "open attacks" by members of senior coalition partners the CDU, Bärbel Bas has stepped down as co-leader of the SPD and as federal labor minister.

She also said a recent death in the family had influenced her decision to resign.

You can read our full report on the latest trial for Chancellor Merz's coalition here .

Welcome to our coverage

Good morning from a crisp, autumnal Bonn!

Today Germany is talking about Bärbel Bas, federal labor minister and co-chair of the Social Democrats resigning amid coalition tensions with Chancellor Merz's Christian Democrats (CDU).

Additionally, Bavaria's Markus Söder has called on CDU members who voted for the election of a far-right parliamentary speaker in Saxony-Anhalt come clean about breaking the "firewall" against supporting the AfD.

All this and morning coming up in today's edition.

stories.title: Resisting the Menace of Federal Data Consolidation
stories.summary: In the past two years, the federal government has unlawfully consolidated data exposing our private information. This consolidation has been chaotic but generally came in three rolling waves: It started with DOGE, moved to agency-to-agency data sharing with ICE, and then attempted data-driven purges of state voter rolls. We all deserve to live in a world where the data we use to pay our taxes, receive benefits, and vote is not combined and weaponized against us. The amalgamation of data leads to mistakes, abuses, and a lack of trust in institutions meant to protect us. Overall, it can chill our participation in society. This is particularly true for groups disfavored by this administration—especially immigrants and protesters. Congress highlighted similar abuses—including the creation of enemies lists and snooping on activists and federal employees—following the McCarthy and Watergate eras. And the increasing use of computers to magnify those harms led Congress to pass a slate of protections like the federal Privacy Act of 1974. The good news is that many people have stepped forward to resist the federal government’s unprecedented and unlawful data consolidations. Many groups, including EFF, have filed lawsuits to enforce our data privacy laws, and many states have, too. Legislators at the federal and state levels have worked to expose and oppose these surveillance programs. And many people have protested for their right to data privacy. Existing data privacy protections have been essential in the past two years, but they can be improved . This should include: narrowing loopholes and increasing enforcement in existing laws, limiting the government’s purchase of data on the commercial market, and passing a comprehensive consumer privacy law. stories.title: Organizing in the Town at Oakland Tech Week
stories.summary: EFF was thrilled to join organizers, advocates, and activists in the East Bay for the second annual Oakland Tech Week last week. We are grateful to our friends at MediaJustice and Upturn for inviting us co-present this all-day event, “Building Beyond Big Tech: Organizing Oakland’s Future” , on Sept. 30. The event, hosted by the Kapor Center in downtown Oakland, offered a unique chance to spend time with people across The Town and the Bay Area working to create a better future for everyone. “We’re at this truly consequential moment,” said EFF executive director Nicole Ozer, in her speech kicking off the day’s events. “We know that in this community’s work—and communities across the country—our ability to ensure that technology empowers rather than oppresses is fundamental to the future of countries, our livelihoods, and, literally, our lives.” We also participated in a panel on the state of play in California, moderated by MediaJustice executive director Steven Renderos. Director of State Affairs Hayley Tsukayama joined reporter Khari Johnson of CalMatters and Crystal Zemero of People Over Billionaires to talk about the landscape at the state level. The day also included smaller conversations focused on building better tech and fine-tuning messaging, facilitated by our colleagues at MediaJustice. Seeing the people—our neighbors—who are fighting back against surveillance in their communities was inspiring. They’re casting doubt on the claims large technology companies make about what’s happening in their neighborhoods. They’re speaking up at council meetings and rallies. They’re seeking changes that would give their workplaces and neighborhoods a better, safer relationship with technology. stories.title: The Social Reckoning review – Aaron Sorkin’s jittery sequel with all-new evil puppet Zuckerberg
stories.summary: Jeremy Strong’s slow-talking Facebook founder turns into a cameo, background to a thriller about a whistleblower that somehow never mentions Trump Here is a film for all those people who solemnly deplore social media in conversation but haven’t quite got round to deleting their accounts. Sixteen years have gone by since The Social Network , written by Aaron Sorkin and directed by David Fincher; this was the addictive, obsessive-compulsive movie about the birth of Facebook in Harvard’s macho-competitive cauldron of student sexism and nerdy self-pity, starring Jesse Eisenberg as the fast-talking, arrogant, not-necessarily-evil genius Mark Zuckerberg. Now Sorkin is back with a sequel of sorts, directing his own script – and now Zuckerberg is basically evil, but also weirdly slow talking, as if all the zinging, smart-alecky Sorkinesque dialogue energy of the first film has been siphoned away in early middle age and dispersed among the insurgents in the new cast. Sorkin’s jittery, funny, syncopated style is unmistakable, as distinctive in its way as David Mamet, although he has one joke about “spatula” being a Yiddish word that he has borrowed from Philip Roth’s Portnoy’s Complaint . It is the story of how in 2021, Zuckerberg’s Facebook empire was challenged by courageous whistleblower-employee Frances Haugen and Wall Street Journal investigative reporter Jeff Horwitz, who were on a mission to tell the world how Zuckerberg, scared by falling revenue, changed the algorithm so that engagement was supercharged by rage bait and hate speech, malice and envy. Facebook, moreover, didn’t factcheck political ads, thus driving a huge, nationwide surge in extremist groups and teen bullying and becoming a major player in the Capitol riots. (Having said that, this film does not say aloud the word “Trump” and rather cravenly declines to specify Maga activity.) Continue reading...

stories.title: What the £350 Grand Theft Auto ‘collector’s box’ says about the escalating cost of gaming
stories.summary: The launch of a collector’s box hints at a new reality: the kinds of games I grew up with are becoming a luxury item, locked behind a forbidding spending barrier • Don’t get Pushing Buttons delivered to your inbox? Sign up here As a parent (and partner) to a habitual collector, I do feel like an unwelcome portion of my life is occupied by an endless war against stuff. Surfaces in my home ceaselessly accumulate piles of random objects: a JoyCon wrist strap, a sticker sheet, an unidentifiable plastic piece of a toy or gizmo, an Xbox 360 controller with no batteries, cases for Switch cartridges lost down the side of the sofa … Stuff encroaches everywhere, especially in a gaming household. Much as I regret the imminent disappearance of physical games , I do not regret the extra space I have in my attic as a result of switching almost entirely to downloaded games over the last decade or so. Speaking of the imminent disappearance of physical games: Rockstar recently announced a £350 ($400) “collector’s box” of Grand Theft Auto 6 goodies … that doesn’t include the game itself. Not even a download code. The Grand Theft Auto VI: The Goodtime State – Vice City Collection, to give it its full and unwieldy name, contains a hat, a bag, a pair of sunglasses, a figurine, a poster and more, including a mirror and a “swizzle spoon” that looks, unambigiously, like a cocaine spoon. stories.body:
Analysts say fuel will take weeks to ship and quantity is too small to affect prices, while full deal is unlikely to be met given damage to Russian refineries

Trump announces partial ceasefire but Zelenskyy says deal is ‘news to me’

Donald Trump’s deal with Vladimir Putin to temporarily lift sanctions on US imports of Russian diesel will have little “meaningful” effect on motorists and businesses in the US and overseas, energy and foreign policy analysts have predicted.

The US president infuriated Volodymyr Zelenskyy when he announced the deal on Friday, writing on Truth Social that the agreement with his Russia counterpart to supply millions of tonnes of diesel was essential to reduce fuel prices in the US, which have soared after his decision to go to war against Iran.

The package announced by Trump involves 300,000 tonnes of diesel released immediately “to the American and global marketplace” followed by 500,000 tonnes in November and a further 1m tonnes after that. The 300,000 figure equates to about three-quarters of what the US would use in a day, according to calculations using figures from the US Energy Information Administration .

“Diesel prices for Americans and, indeed, the world, will be COMING DOWN, IN RECORD NUMBERS, AND FAST! Lower prices for Americans, especially our Great Farmers, Ranchers, and Truckers, is my greatest priority,” Trump posted.

However, experts suggested that the quantities involved – and the time it will take for the supplies to arrive in the US – is “too little, too late” to affect current high diesel prices, which observers have linked to challenging Republican party polling numbers before next month’s midterm elections.

US prices have surged by almost 70% since the start of the Iran war, to about $6.30 a gallon , according to American Automobile Association. In the UK, the average price of diesel climbed to a record £2 a litre earlier in October, and sat just below that mark on Friday.

Ashley Kelty, an energy analyst with the investment bank Panmure Liberum, said: “It is not going to have any impact on prices. The first amount [due to be shipped to the US] is so small.

“They are going to have to charter vessels, load them and transport the cargo to the US. That will take about three weeks – so we are pretty much at the end of the month and about a week before the midterms.”

The US Treasury secretary, Scott ⁠Bessent, said on Sunday: “This is ​good ‌for the ​American ​people … bringing these diesel prices down.”

However, Kelty said the diesel shipments would also cause complications in a global supply chain, including multinational companies having to work out which of its supplies originated from Russia and therefore might breach sanctions in other jurisdictions, including Europe .

The US Treasury suspended sanctions on Russian diesel exports until 7 April as part of the deal, while keeping in place other sanctions on Russian products.

Zelenskyy described Trump’s deal as a “weak decision”, saying it would encourage Russia to keep attacking Ukraine, but Trump then blamed Kyiv’s strikes on Russian energy infrastructure for rising fuel prices. Trump said Ukraine neeeded “a new leader” .

On Sunday, Zelenskyy said he would be ready to stop hitting Russian oil refineries if Russia curbed its attacks on Ukrainian energy infrastructure.

Trump later posted on Truth Social: “Effective immediately, there is an ENERGY CEASEFIRE in the War between Russia and Ukraine . Both parties have agreed. Do not break it! Thank you for your attention to this matter.”

Maximilian Hess, the founder of the political risk consultancy Enmetena Advisory and a fellow at the Foreign Policy Research Institute, said: “It will not have any meaningful domestic US effect or international effect given its full terms are highly unlikely to be met as a result of the impact of Ukrainian drone strikes on Russian refining which have limited its diesel output.

“The whole point of the deal for Putin is that it fails, which he can blame on Ukraine and thus stoke tensions between Trump and Zelenskyy. Indeed, it’s already working.”

stories.title: Citroen revives the 2CV for an electric age
stories.summary: The French firm is reinventing the classic model as carmakers come under pressure from Chinese rivals.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Published 11 October 2026

French carmaker Citroen has brought back its 2CV brand in a bid to boost sales of electric cars in a difficult market.

The new model, unveiled at the Paris Motor Show, is a small city runabout with retro styling which harks back to one of the company's most famous designs.

As a "concept car" intended to show Citroen's direction of travel, it is not yet ready to go on sale but the plan is to have a version in showrooms by 2028.

As they face mounting competition from Chinese manufacturers, Citroen and other European brands are exploiting their heritage as a means of selling modern motors.

Farmers’ favourite

Citroen chief executive Xavier Chardon described the new car as "a modern, ingenious and refreshing response to the mobility challenges of tomorrow".

The original Citroen 2CV was launched in 1948, as Europe was recovering from the ravages of World War Two. It was designed as a cheap, robust way for French farmers and country folk to get around.

The car had high wheel arches and soft suspension, letting it travel across a ploughed field or rough roads - as legend would have it, without breaking a tray of duck eggs.

Its high roof let drivers wear a hat at the wheel. It was easy to drive and simple to repair.

The car was so popular, it remained in production for more than 40 years. Over time, it went from being a utilitarian tool for the countryside to a cult classic, and a favourite of hippies and counter-culturalists.

Fans of Citroën's 2CV hold annual meet-ups such as this muddy gathering in Switzerland

Now, Citroen wants to draw on that heritage to sell an electric, small city car that is expected to sell for about £13,000.

The look of the new 2CV may well evolve as Citroen develops its design. But as it stands, it shares plenty of styling features with its famous predecessor.

The high, flared wheel arches, the tall, curved roof and the eye-like headlights are all reminders of the original "deux chevaux" or "two horses".

By using memories of an old car to sell a new one, Citroen is following a well-travelled road.

VW notoriously brought back the Beetle in the late 1990s, with limited success.

BMW's Minis have always carried styling designed to hark back to the very British original. Fiat has been selling a retro-styled Fiat 500 for the past two decades.

Retro-nostalgia

But the retro-nostalgia trend has accelerated recently, as carmakers have looked for ways to sell electric cars to sceptical consumers.

Citroen's French rival, Renault, has led the charge. It started with the Renault 5 E-Tech, which visually echoed the distinctive boxy styling of the original Renault 5, once an ever-present sight on French streets. It has since revived the Renault 4 and Twingo brands as well.

VW has the distinctive ID-Buzz minivan, a throwback to the classic T2 Transporter, while Ford is working on a new EV which is widely expected to be called the Fiesta.

Rachel Burgess, senior editor of Autocar magazine, thinks it is a strategy that makes perfect sense.

"It's a brilliant differentiator from all-new car brands", she says. "An older audience might remember the originals and feel warmly towards them, and a younger audience might find an appeal in the retro aspect."

Finding new ways to make cars appealing has become more important than ever, at a time when European manufacturers are facing growing competition from Chinese brands.

"Many in the industry believe the big automotive players in Europe…face a very serious existential threat from aggressive Chinese manufacturers," says David Leggett, automotive editor at Global Data.

Back to the future: VW looked to the past when designing its ID-Buzz minivan

In this hostile business environment, heritage and nostalgia could prove to be powerful weapons for more established brands, thinks automotive researcher and author Dr Paul Nieuwenhuis.

"In a world where a wave of credible decent quality Chinese EVs are hitting Europe, linking European designs back to their history while using the latest powertrain technology is something the Chinese cannot do," he says.

"The Chinese can establish new design trends, but there is limited history there."

But Leggett thinks Citroen will need more than a heady whiff of nostalgia to turn its new car into a best-seller.

"A reimagined Citroën 2CV should give a big nod to its ancestor - especially on price and design simplicity as well as visual cues," he says.

"But it also needs to be a credible modern electric car in terms of functionality and features, with widespread appeal."
