stories.title: Fridges in French supermarkets hit by cyber attack
stories.summary: Hundreds of stores were targeted by the overnight hack, which spoiled fresh and frozen food estimated to be worth millions of euros.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Published 12 October 2026, 15:30 BST

Hundreds of French supermarkets have been hit by a cyber attack that caused their fridges and freezers to heat up, spoiling fresh and frozen food estimated to be worth millions of euros.

Hackers gained control of the software that regulates the temperatures of the refrigeration units, forcing some to warm to 50C (120F) overnight.

The chief executive of Coopérative U said several of its supermarkets had been hit by the "extremely serious and unprecedented" attack.

More than 100 of the chain's supermarkets were targeted, while at least 300 stores from Intermarché and its Netto brand were affected, according to the AFP news agency.

Other major food retailers including Carrefour, Monoprix and E.Leclerc were also hit by the attack, which targeted software provided by Danish engineering firm Danfoss.

The software allows retailers to manage their cold units remotely.

Normally, supermarket freezers go through a short period of defrosting overnight, in which temperatures rise slightly. But here, the hackers ordered the units to heat up and stay hot.

Danfoss said the affected cold units were older models whose security software could not be updated to ward off a risk they had identified.

The full scale of the attack is unclear, but figures supplied by individual chains suggest about 500 stores were affected out of 15,000 or so overall in France.

Carrefour said fridges in 80 of its 6,000 stores were hacked, while Monoprix said 5% of its more than 400 stores had been hit, with food removed from sale if its condition could not be guaranteed.

In a statement to the BBC, Mousquetaires Group - which owns Intermarché and Netto - said some fresh and frozen food display units remained out of service on Monday afternoon.

The stores had "taken all necessary precautions to remove the products from these units", it said, adding that staff were working to restock the shelves "as soon as possible".

Intermarché said its fridges had heated up to 50C for six hours overnight into Monday, and the retailer had thrown away all the affected food to avoid health risks, the Reuters news agency reported.

As a result of the attack, managers arriving at branches of several supermarket chains on Monday morning were hit by a wave of hot air from the freezers. In some places there were even small fires.

French broadcaster BFMTV published an image showing a freezer in an ice cream aisle displaying a temperature of 26.5C.

Two supermarkets in the Alsace region reported losses of €270,000 (£228,000) between them, the broadcaster added, meaning the nationwide total could run into the millions.

French prosecutors have opened a specific cyber-crime investigation into the incident, which the Paris prosecutor's office called a "large-scale cyber-attack affecting the refrigerators of several major food retail chains across France".

European Food Commissioner Christophe Hansen condemned the hack in a post on X and added: "Food security requires more attention at all levels. Because the weaponisation of food has become a reality."

In a post on X, Coopérative chief executive Dominique Schelcher said staff were "fully mobilised, in co-ordination with refrigeration specialists, to restore the situation as quickly as possible".

He called for an investigation into the hack and said targeting equipment essential to the French food supply was "unacceptable".

stories.title: AI minister warns 'likely' UK's cyber defences will be breached
stories.summary: Kanishka Narayan said the government will use advanced AI to strengthen the UK against cyber attacks.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Published 12 October 2026, 13:11 BST

The UK's AI minister has warned it is "likely, if not inevitable" the country's cyber defences will at some point be breached.

Speaking at a press conference, Kanishka Narayan pointed to an incident of a rogue OpenAI agent hacking an Australian government website in June.

He said while no medical records are known to have been accessed in the attack, the incident should still "concern us".

Narayan said the government plans to put advanced AI to work to combat the threat, as he set out how the government plans to prepare for any serious future incidents.

The minister said the move would build on two existing pilots which have helped identify and fix over 1,000 vulnerabilities across government systems.

He said his message to the largest companies behind the world's most powerful AI systems was: "Listen when your scientists warn of serious dangers. Investigate unexpected behaviour. And if you cannot adequately control the risks, do not release the system."

In his speech, Narayan also confirmed scientists at the UK's AI watchdog, the AI Security Institute (AISI), were conducting "rigorous evaluations" of the latest generation of advanced AI models to "identify risks early" and "to test robust safeguards to help keep people safe".

AI testing

AISI began evaluating risks of the latest frontier AI models, prior to their public release, shortly after it was established in November 2023.

But it was reported in September , external that the White House had asked some leading US labs not to share their models with the research organisation until its own tests were completed.

The move was viewed at the time as a blow to AISI - which has been championed by the UK government and its partners for advancing open, constructive and collaborative AI testing.

Microsoft president Brad Smith recently told the BBC the institute had helped cement the UK as the country best-placed to drive forward global regulation.

On Monday, Narayan said that in the last few weeks, the government had worked with the US "to retain access for Britain's AISI to the most powerful AI models before they are released".

He also said the UK would also look into creating stronger protections through the Cyber Security and Resilience bill, particularly at how serious AI incidents can be identified and reported.

Nuala Polo, UK Public Policy Lead at the Ada Lovelace Institute, said the announcement committed the government to "very little".

"Stronger protections will be 'considered', strengthening the Cyber Bill 'explored' and near-miss reporting 'looked at', with the detail to come later," she said.

"There is no new regulatory power, no timetable and no obligation on AI developers."

Regulation

The announcement follows a series of incidents involving AI agents across major firms such as OpenAI and Anthropic acting outside human control and hacking into external systems.

On 9 September, Evan Hubinger, a top safety researcher at Anthropic, warned in a post on X that AI is advancing so quickly he believed there is a greater than 10% chance it "could kill all humans" within the next decade.

The bosses of the US-based AI giants such as Anthropic, OpenAI and Google DeepMind have all backed the idea of an AI development slowdown .

However, there are currently no global safety rules in place to regulate the companies and their technology. President Trump has called for the sector to regulate itself so that US firms do not lose out to Chinese rivals.

Speaking to the BBC following the announcement, Narayan said the UK needed "to be confident... as a country" when questioned as to how the government can make foreign AI firms abide by UK rules.

"We have the capability, we have the trust, and we have a government that is right on the side of the British public in making sure we don't just have laws but the ability to enforce those laws," he said.

"What we are focused on is delivering the right outcome for the British public, where the law was the answer."

On the question of whether the UK should have its own sovereign AI frontier model, the minister said he was "focused" on securing British sovereignty, which meant "placing the right set of investments".

"It's British chips being made here. It's British models outside of just language, looking at things like drug discovery, materials discovery, computer vision and its areas of adoption, including AI, security and cyber-security," he said.

stories.summary: The Environment Agency has warned approximately 6.3 million homes and businesses in England remain at risk of flooding.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Published 11 October 2026

The government has launched a new taskforce to respond to extreme weather, including the risk of flooding this winter.

After a summer of record-breaking temperatures, the group will meet this week to assess how prepared the UK is for what the Met Office described as the "heightened potential" for wet, windy, stormy weather in the coming months.

"We're facing extreme weather, with flood and drought intertwined but the government is taking decisive action," Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs (Defra) Minister Emma Hardy said in a statement ahead of the meeting.

The Environment Agency has warned approximately 6.3 million homes and businesses in England remain at risk of flooding.

Defra will host the first meeting on Wednesday, bringing together the Met Office, Environment Agency and mayoral authorities as well as the farming, water and insurance industries.

Hardy said: "This will put communities and businesses at the heart of our work and will make sure the UK is ready for whatever the weather brings next."

The government has committed at least £10.5bn until 2036 to protect homes, businesses and critical infrastructure from the growing threat of flooding.

The Met Office has said the current seasonal outlook suggests an increased likelihood of wetter than average conditions during autumn, in part due to the El Niño weather event.

It has warned that this year's iteration of the climate phenomenon is likely to be the strongest in living memory, with the peak not expected until the end of the year.

The Environment Agency has said that while flooding is not guaranteed, the odds of repeated storms, prolonged rain and saturated catchments are higher than average this winter.

It has urged households to check their flood risk, sign up to alerts and make a flood plan to prepare for any emergencies.

The warnings follow 12 months of extreme weather across the UK, with the summer of 2026 the country's hottest on record .

Last winter brought four named storms to the UK - Bram, Goretti, Ingrid and Chandra - and several significant flooding events, with the Met Office reporting that England received 42% more rainfall than its winter average.

stories.title: Amazon has over 1 million robot workers. What’s next for human employees?
stories.summary: The second-largest corporate employer has bet big on robot workers to scale.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
The second-largest corporate employer has bet big on robot workers to scale.

No organization in the world operates more robots than Amazon. The company already has more than 1 million robots working in warehouses around the clock to make tens of millions of same-day and one-day package deliveries happen on a daily basis—and Amazon is poised to significantly grow that robotic fleet in the coming years as it establishes new factories to churn out increasingly more capable robot workers.

Despite deploying so many robots, Amazon is also the second-largest corporate employer in the world, with more than 1.5 million full-time and part-time human workers, according to its 2025 annual report . Amazon executives say that the growing robot fleet has eased the burden on its human workforce by taking on the toughest fulfillment center tasks that carry the greatest risks of physical fatigue and injury. But labor advocacy groups and independent researchers point to evidence suggesting that warehouse automation driven by AI is not all upside for the humans who work alongside robots.

“For the last 100 years, most of the automation that we’ve seen usually happens away from workers—you’re taking that high-risk task away from the worker, and you’re doing so in a way that is not physically proximate,” Brian Greenwood , professor of business at George Mason University, told Ars. “The rise of collaborative robots really changes that dynamic for two reasons: one is that it is physically proximate, and two, the robot has the ability to dictate the pace of work.”

In many ways, robotics and AI are well suited to the relentless pace of work that is already happening inside e-commerce fulfillment centers. Amazon’s promise of speedy deliveries for its 200 million Prime subscribers in particular requires hundreds of thousands of human employees to speedily assemble and ship out customer orders that often combine a dizzying array of products.

Much of the work in fulfillment centers also frequently involves “dull, dirty and dangerous” tasks that people may prefer to hand over to robots. The injury and illness rate for workers in the US warehouse sector has typically been more than double the average across all industries, according to the US Occupational Safety and Health Administration .

“You have almost 2 million people working in the warehousing sector in the United States, and it’s characterized by very high turnover and very high workplace injury rates,” said Greenwood.

But robots are still far from capable of handling the many different tasks that human workers can perform. So Amazon still has a massive human workforce working in tandem with the company’s growing fleet of wheeled robots and robotic arms—and workplaces can get complicated when humans are expected to keep pace with robotic counterparts.

Amazon’s robotic era

Amazon has rapidly built its robotic fleet following the pivotal decision to acquire the robotics company Kiva Systems in 2012. Kiva was among the earliest companies to pioneer wheeled mobile robots that bring racks of items to warehouse workers, instead of requiring people to continually walk around grabbing items off of shelves inside fulfillment centers.

Since the acquisition, Kiva was renamed Amazon Robotics and has focused on deploying an array of mobile robots and robotic arms that Amazon primarily manufactures in-house at facilities in Massachusetts. This year, the company also announced it would build additional production factories in Austin, Texas, and Greenwood, Indiana , to churn out even more robots in the future.

“There’s a theme of how we look at the challenges that we can help our associates and our employees with, and how we can make our customers’ lives better through these technologies,” Scott Dresser , vice president of Amazon Robotics, told Ars. “Each step of the way, [we are] tackling a hard or deep set of technical challenges to achieve that goal.”

Most of Amazon’s million-robot fleet still consists of those wheeled mobile robots . The company claims that its robotic Sequoia system can identify and store items up to 75 percent faster at fulfillment centers by coordinating swarms of such robots. Hercules and Titan robots, the size of a pool table or a baby grand piano, respectively, roam warehouse aisles to retrieve tall fabric shelving units called pods packed with plastic tote crates and bring them to human employees at various workstations.

Such mobile robots typically follow grid lines of stickers laid out on the floor and stay within fenced-in areas away from human employees. But the newest mobile robot, called Proteus , has sensors that allow it to operate safely around humans and other objects in a more free-roaming role.

Those swarms of mobile robots traveling through narrow lanes between rows of storage pods can also sometimes create robotic traffic jams. That is why Amazon began coordinating its robots using a suite of AI foundation models collectively named DeepFleet , which can help predict potential robot congestion ahead of time.

More recently, Amazon has been deploying a growing number of robotic arms that can grab items stowed high up inside inventory pods, sort packages and place them in carts or on top of mobile robots, and handle the many different individual products that Amazon customers order when shopping online.

The company expects to more than double its existing fleet of robotic arms this year, according to Amazon CFO Brian Olsavsky in a July earnings call. When Ars sought clarification, Dresser described the current number of deployed robotic arms as being in the single-digit thousands.

The robotic arms race

Amazon first bought third-party robotic arms to help lift and stack heavy pallets and bins inside its fulfillment centers. But the first robotic arm developed in-house by Amazon Robotics to sort individual mailer envelopes and boxes from cluttered piles, called Robin , began testing in 2021 before debuting at a facility in Lakeland, Florida, in 2022.

“With Robin, it was really that first attempt at taking a number of customer orders all in a jumble and building the advanced robotics to identify the items in that scene, to strategize on how to pick them up and build a motion plan that would be successful in placing it down on one of our mobile drive units,” Dresser explained.

The robotic arm uses eight suction cups to pick up individual packages. But before it takes any action, the robot’s software analyzes a top-down view of the conveyor belt cluttered with packages and quickly ranks possible picking actions.

In a 2023 research paper, the Amazon Robotics team described having developed several picking strategies for the robots to follow early on—but each had its own limitations. One strategy that prioritized picking larger packages encountered challenges when smaller packages lay on top of or overlapped with larger ones. Another strategy that favored picking up packages near the top of piles would fail in practice to retrieve “unreachable picks” and partially buried packages.

Improvements came from replacing such hand-crafted algorithms with an AI approach known as machine learning. The machine learning model initially trained on more than 394,000 picking actions from deployed robotic arms to estimate pick probabilities of success, and then used an online pick ranker to prioritize optimal actions for the Robin robots.

The best machine-learning method in that trial achieved a 93.73 percent success rate compared to 92.28 percent success for the best-performing traditional algorithm. That may seem trivial at first glance, but it meant the machine-learning method resulted in about 16,500 fewer failed picks than the traditional method during a work period involving more than 1 million total picks. That matters for an operation like Amazon’s that prioritizes speed and efficiency at scale.

The Amazon Robotics team further showed how such a machine-learning method could reduce the failed pick rate by 20 percent during an experiment involving 2 million picks by robotic workstations set up to resemble the operations of Amazon’s Robin fleet. They presented this work at the International Symposium on Experimental Robotics in July 2025.

Next up was Cardinal, a robotic arm that can place packages weighing up to 50 pounds into wheeled carts that are eventually brought to Amazon trucks waiting in loading docks. These robots first began operating at a facility in Nashville, Tennessee, in November 2022.

“Think of it as a game of Tetris : You’re sorting packages, and you’re placing them into the cart, and you want to be able to pack that as densely as you possibly can,” Dresser told Ars. “Dense containers are great from a sustainability perspective and from a transportation cost perspective.”

Cardinal built on lessons learned from Robin’s development in picking up and manipulating packages, while adding the capability to densely pack customer orders into the carts. Amazon has just started to deploy Cardinal in larger numbers and will continue to do so over the next several years, Dresser said.

AI-driven robot successors

Robin and Cardinal can handle several dozen package variations. But the newer Sparrow robotic arm was developed to tackle an even more challenging task—handling the hundreds of millions of products of varying shapes and sizes that can go into customer orders.

Specifically, Sparrow focuses on consolidating items from partially filled container-size totes to create densely packed totes. When items get picked out as customer orders are being fulfilled, Sparrow continually refills the totes.

“When we think about how AI applies to the physical space in robotics, Sparrow was really the first place where we truly deployed foundation models that enabled us to deal with that high diversity of products,” Dresser told Ars.

Such foundation models have helped the Amazon Robotics team to efficiently identify and classify those hundreds of millions of items to develop new robotic strategies for grasping them, Dresser explained. They also eliminated the need for manually coding every single item.

More recently, the Amazon Robotics team has created a foundation model for robotic perception that can handle new, never-before-seen products that may end up in Amazon fulfillment centers. The team also developed a generalized action model compatible with different types of robotic arms that may use varying combinations of suction and finger grasping.

“If you need to build ad hoc perception models for every such task and embodiment, that just doesn’t scale,” Kapil Katyal , a senior applied science manager at Amazon Robotics, said during a presentation attended by Ars at the Intelligent Robots & Systems conference held in Pittsburgh on September 29.

“So one of the initiatives we took up in our team was to design a foundation model which could work for any new embodiment of robots that we deploy, and across all of the perception tasks that we need to perform over those,” Katyal said.

Most of the robotic arms have relied primarily on vision. But Amazon’s newest robotic arm, Vulcan , is the first to combine vision with force feedback sensors capable of providing a sense of touch. This enables the robot to accurately pick out or stow away items within the fabric-covered inventory pods.

“You need to be able to insert an item, create space, or pull something out,” Dresser said. “Those are really hard things to do with traditional non-touch-based systems today, like the suction-based systems that are part of Sparrow.”

Vulcan initially began operating at Amazon fulfillment centers in Spokane, Washington, and Hamburg, Germany, starting in 2025. It is not widely deployed yet, but Dresser said the company expects to scale up use of this robotic arm in 2027.

Parsing the human impact

Each new robot has benefited Amazon’s human workforce, according to the company. For example, Vulcan focuses on picking and stowing items located in the top rows of inventory pods that would otherwise require a person to use a step-ladder, along with handling items located just above the floor. That enables employees to focus on picking and stowing items that are within more comfortable reach.

But investigations by labor advocacy groups, journalists, and the US Congress have painted a less rosy picture of Amazon’s automation drive over the years. The Strategic Organizing Center (SOC), a coalition of trade unions headquartered in Washington, DC, published reports in May 2021 and April 2022 showing higher injury rates at Amazon’s robotic warehouses compared to non-robotic warehouses. That analysis drew on injury data reported by companies to the US government from 2017 through 2020.

“Amazon likes to talk about its latest robots because it doesn’t want to talk about the tens of thousands of Amazon workers who are injured every year due to Amazon’s obsession with maximizing speed and minimizing costs,” Joan Moriarty, director of strategic research and Campaigns at SOC, said in an email to Ars.

The organization also gathered nearly 1,000 responses from Amazon workers in an online survey conducted in February 2021. “Workers consistently report that the presence of robots increases the pace of work expected in Amazon facilities, forcing them to make fast, repetitive motions, substantially increasing the risk of injury,” Moriarty said.

The US Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor and Pensions (HELP) also conducted a 2024 investigation led by Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt). The committee’s report noted how Amazon’s internal data also suggested a link between robotic productivity and increased pressure on human workers, leading to higher injury rates.

Amazon has described these reports as flawed and being reliant on older data predating the deployment of its most modern robots, including the robotic arms that became operational over the past several years. The company also touted improvements in its overall workplace injury rates without detailing any potential differences between robotic and non-automated warehouses.

“All of these claims ignore the fact that since 2019 our Global Recordable Incident Rate has improved 43 percent and our Global Lost Time Incident rate, which includes the most serious injuries that require employees to take time away from work, has improved 70 percent,” an Amazon spokesperson told Ars. “Our consistent year-over-year improvements have worked in parallel with our robotics growth across our operations network.”

The most nuanced findings on Amazon’s automation drive may come from a research study published in the journal ILR Review in April 2025. That analysis showed Amazon’s robotic warehouses had a 40 percent decrease in severe injuries compared to legacy fulfillment centers—which suggests some benefits from having robots take on the most physically challenging and risky tasks.

However, the same study also found that robotic fulfillment centers had a 77 percent increase in less severe injuries associated with physical strain from repetitive motions.

“At least one of the mechanisms by which this appears to be manifesting is through the pace of work, in that pick rates for the robotic fulfillment centers are off the charts higher,” said Greenwood at George Mason University, who was one of the paper’s coauthors.

A faster pace of work driven by partial automation could mean “the robot is dictating the pace of work” and spurring human employees to perform certain repetitive actions more quickly, Greenwood told Ars. “That appears to be what’s driving the strains and the sprains that we observe,” he said.

The study drew in part on Amazon company data obtained by journalists at Reveal and The Center for Investigative Reporting , covering weekly data at more than 150 Amazon warehouses from 2016 through 2019. Although the data is older, Greenwood said the findings are still relevant to Amazon’s ongoing automation efforts.

“I haven’t seen a tremendous amount of evidence to suggest that these dynamics are changing, inasmuch as you still have a tremendous amount of turnover in the warehousing context—and that’s not just Amazon,” Greenwood said.

Greenwood and his colleagues also analyzed online comments posted on Reddit by Amazon fulfillment center employees. In those comments, Amazon employees described work at robotic fulfillment centers as being less physically stressful but also mentally exhausting because of the physical repetitiveness and faster pace associated with higher productivity expectations.

The future of work

An obvious question is whether automation efforts by Amazon and other companies will end up replacing some potential human hires with robots. For its part, Amazon has touted the robotics push as providing new job opportunities for human employees. Fulfillment centers with advanced robotics typically require 30 percent more employees working in reliability, maintenance, and engineering roles, and the new facilities for manufacturing additional robots will also supposedly bring more than 300 jobs each.

“As we recognize that each of these robotics [developments] can change the nature of work, we’re providing opportunities for our employees to upskill and learn some of these things,” said Dresser at Amazon Robotics. “We’ve actually increased the number of robotic maintenance technicians that we have in the network by over 30 percent, and that is a much higher-skilled, higher-compensated job.”

The company has also described its automation efforts as going hand in hand with a growing business that needs more human employees. “As we’ve deployed robots over the past decade, we’ve seen our operational footprint grow, creating hundreds of thousands of jobs as we expanded our network,” the Amazon spokesperson told Ars.

However, there are apparently internal discussions within Amazon about robots potentially reducing the need to hire humans. In October 2025, The New York Times reported on internal strategy documents suggesting that the robotics push could allow the company to reduce projected hiring needs in the United States by more than 160,000 people by 2027 and 600,000 people by 2033. (An Amazon spokesperson responded at the time by saying the documents reflected the views of just one group inside the company.)

Even as Amazon looks to build out its robotic fleet beyond the million-robot mark, discussions about the company’s workplace safety and working conditions are unlikely to go away. Although just a very small fraction of Amazon’s hundreds of thousands of employees have unionized in the United States, labor unions have “traditionally served a very good role in terms of improving worker safety,” Greenwood said.

“Now, obviously, I understand that firms are not always excited to engage in that conversation, and I can’t say that would solve the problem here,” Greenwood told Ars. “But developing a better relationship between management and labor is usually the best path forward to try to figure out how to reduce these injury rates, which would have benefits for Amazon as well.”

The first Amazon Labor Union that was organized among workers at a warehouse in Staten Island, New York, in April 2022, has been pushing what it describes as a Safety Bill of Rights that outlines changes it would like to see to make their workplace safer. The image that accompanies the document declares: “We are not robots.”

stories.title: MPs seek to overturn ruling that stops police being sued for failings
stories.summary: MPs are seeking to stop immunity applying when police fabricate evidence or are dishonest or negligent.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Published 11 October 2026

Backbench MPs are seeking to roll back a court ruling they say will have "devastating consequences" for victims of crime by preventing them taking legal action against the police, even when there have been grave investigative failings.

The 2025 Court of Appeal judgment, which applies to England and Wales, held that police officers are immune from civil litigation both in their role as witnesses, and for conduct or statements they make when carrying out criminal investigations.

Conservative Andrew Mitchell and Labour's Jess Phillips have submitted an amendment to a bill being debated in Parliament next week seeking to counteract the ruling.

Separately, the judgment could also be overturned at a Supreme Court appeal this month.

The MPs are seeking to stop immunity applying, including in cases where police have fabricated evidence, been dishonest or negligent, and where there has been a reckless disclosure of confidential information relating to victims.

The ruling came in a case brought by a victim of serious domestic violence who fled her abuser for a secret refuge, but Sussex Police included her new address in a file sent to the Crown Prosecution Service (CPS) without sufficiently flagging its confidentiality.

A CPS lawyer subsequently disclosed her address in court during a bail hearing, thereby revealing it to her abuser. As a result, she had to flee again.

The woman said the disclosure of her address had meant the place she was supposed to be safe "no longer felt safe at all" and she was still living with the impact of what happened and that loss of security.

She brought claims against both the police and CPS, arguing their failure placed her in fear for her life, compelled her to leave her home, caused her to suffer loss of earnings, and resulted in her developing a psychiatric injury. Her claims were initially rejected, reinstated on appeal, then struck out again.

The key issue was who could be held legally responsible for what happened, and who would benefit from legal immunity. Witnesses and lawyers have what is known as "core immunity" for things they say in court, so that they can speak freely there.

The Court of Appeal ruling further expanded such immunity, holding that it extends to an extremely broad range of police activity, including conduct or statements which are part of an investigation leading to a potential prosecution

Most types of legal claim are thus blocked by this immunity, including cases about serious human rights abuses and data breaches, and there are no exemptions for unjustifiable conduct.

Officers can still be prosecuted in the criminal courts and held accountable by police misconduct processes.

Ali Kololo is suing the Metropolitan Police after he was wrongly convicted in Kenya

The amendment by Mitchell and Phillips, which will be debated on Tuesday, states that, except while acting as witnesses, no immunity applies to actions by police officers in preparation for criminal proceedings, including in cases where there are specified grave failings.

Mitchell told BBC News the "police misconduct immunity created by the Court of Appeal's ruling" was extremely concerning and that if "we fail to close this legal loophole there will be devastating consequences for victims".

He cited the case of Ali Kololo, saying his life was "ruined by a wrongful conviction secured, in large part, by the Metropolitan Police".

Mr Kololo, a Kenyan woodcutter, spent 11 years in jail after being wrongfully convicted of assisting a gang that attacked two British tourists in Kenya in 2011 - one of whom was murdered. He was sentenced to death following a trial in Kenya, at which a senior Met officer who was called to appear as a prosecution witness omitted key evidence.

Mr Kololo - who is represented by human rights group, Reprieve - is suing the Met, but the force has said it will rely on the legal principle of core immunity in defending the claim, a position likely to be bolstered by the Court of Appeal ruling.

A Met spokesperson said the force would not comment on the ongoing civil claim, but said its thoughts were with Mr Kololo, the victims of the crime and their families.

Kate Ellis, from the Centre for Women's Justice, told the BBC forces may now argue they cannot be "held legally responsible at all for serious mistakes made in a criminal investigation" and it could lead to an "accountability gap" where police forces who fail to investigate rapists, stalkers or domestic abusers "face no consequences for their failings".

A government spokesperson said: "The home secretary and lord chancellor commissioned a review into police accountability following long-standing concerns from policing leaders, officers, victims and their families that the current system is not fit for purpose. Any changes to how the police are treated should be considered alongside the wider findings of this review."

Sussex Police and the National Police Chiefs Council both declined to comment at this time.

stories.body:
Closing post

Time to wrap up.

Friday has marked a brief reprieve for oil prices, with Brent crude having been down as much as 1.3% mid-morning. Prices are now around 0.3% lower at $103.87 per barrel.

Prices eased overnight on news that US president Donald Trump had pledged not to attack Iran ahead of the US midterm elections, which take place on 3 November.

That was on top of news that news that China is set ⁠to resume fuel exports, after a pause in deliveries during the country’s Golden Week holiday. That offset pressure from Hurricane Isaias , which expected to disrupt oil supplies in the US Gulf coast. There was also some reprieve for motorists, with diesel prices having dropped below £2 per litre There was also a major deal struck by the EU to “moderate” sales of Chinese hybrid electric cars in the EU, that officials said marked a “global first” and could reduce sales of Chinese plug-in hybrid cars by “several million” in the next four years.

Meanwhile, in the UK, shares in Airtel Money began conditional trading on the London Stock Exchange, marking the biggest float in five years. However, it was the worst performing stock on the FTSE 100, down 5.23%. That’s all from us today. Thanks for reading and have a good weekend. -KM

EU reaches landmark deal to 'moderate' sales of Chinese hybrid cars

The EU says it has reached a landmark deal with China to “moderate” sales of Chinese hybrid electric cars in the EU.

It is global first, trade commissioner Maroš Šefčovič, told reporters.

The deal “opens the prospect of cutting China’s export [of hybrids] by more than a half”, he said during a press conference in Beijing, adding:

double quotation mark It is the first time that China has accepted to moderate its exports without going through the prior [trade investigations].

It could go so far as to reduce sales of Chinese plug-in hybrid cars by “several million” in the next four years.

“There are different techniques on how you can do these things,” Šefčovič, said without revealing further details.

He said he wanted to first present the plan to EU leaders - he will brief ambassadors on Sunday morning ahead of a leaders summit on Thursday.

Sefcovic added that the Chinese had recognised the political pressure building Europe with “literally thousand of job losses” and EU leaders “clearly expecting very fast action” from the EU to curb the flood of imports from China.

He said he put “so much emphasis” on today’s negotiations because it was “very difficult to stop a trade war” once it started.

He added that the deal had been “very, very hard to accomplish”:

double quotation mark This is the result of very intense, work. And and it reflects also the appreciation of the situation on both sides. The European car industry is under a lot of stress. And therefore this step was absolutely crucial. But I think that what we agreed is fair, we are working in a full compliance with WTO methodology.

Shein , the online fast-fashion retailer founded in China, increased sales in the UK by just over a quarter last year, overtaking its British rival Asos, Sarah Butler reports.

The company, whose global parent group listed on the Hong Kong stock exchange valued at just over $26bn (£19.6bn) last month, increased sales at its UK division by 26% to £2.58bn, according to accounts filed at Companies House.

Pre-tax profits rose 18% to £45.2m even as the number of people employed by the group in the UK, mostly in sales and marketing, rose to 113 from 91 a year before.

The company paid £11.2m in current tax – understood to be mainly corporation tax – up from £9.6m a year before.

Shein said sales had been helped by a marketing partnership with the Wireless and Creamfields music festivals, a pop-up shop on London’s Oxford Street and Christmas gift events in Edinburgh, Manchester and Liverpool as well as London.

Read more here:

Wall Street is open for trading, and major indexes have followed Europe higher:

Nasdaq is up 0.55%

S&P 500 is up 0.29%

Dow is up 0.13%

After it emerged that China reached an “understanding” with the EU on trade , the Chinese ministry of commerce, led by Wang Wentao, has said the country is: “willing... to continue facilitating the approval of export licenses for rare earths and permanent magnets destined for the EU.”

While they acknowledged “differences” between them, the two sides were committed to maintaining trade and to hold a further meeting in March.

China said both sides would adhere to “procedures concerning company price undertakings” of hybrid cars, Beijing’s commerce ministry said, citing a joint statement, suggesting a deal to find minimum prices for hybrid cars exported to the EU.

The talks follow months of rising tensions between the 27-nation EU and the Asian powerhouse that threatened to escalate into a trade war.

EU trade commissioner Maroš Šefčovič had said it was “crucial” that the talks deliver “tangible outcomes”, after he met with Wang on Thursday.

Maroš Šefčovič said earlier in the day that the EU’s trade deficit with running at around £1bn a day (€1.18bn) every day, was “unsustainable”.

China reaches "understanding" with EU on trade

Breaking: China has reached an “understanding” with the EU , to avert deterioration in trade tensions a fter two days of talks in Beijing, according to a Chinese statement.

EU trade commissioner Maroš Šefčovič i s due to hold a press conference around 3pm CET, but China says the two sides of agreed a 16 point agreement allowing for a relaxation of restrictions on rare earth exports from China to the EU in return for concessions on electric vehicle exports.

Diesel falls below £2 per litre as oil prices ease

Diesel prices have gone under £2 a litre, providing some momentary relief from climbing fuel prices.

However, the RAC notes that prices are still significantly higher than they were before the US launched its war on Iran, leaving households paying much more every time they fill up their tanks.

RAC head of policy Simon Williams said:

double quotation mark While it’s positive to see the average cost of a litre of diesel dipping back below £2 a litre, we’re a long way from being out of the woods when it comes to high fuel prices. Diesel remains around 57p a litre higher than before the US/Iran conflict, and petrol 42p higher – meaning households are paying £31 and £23 more respectively every time they fill up a family-sized car. And as things stand, this year is still set to be the second most expensive year on record for drivers.

Williams went on to say that prime minister Andy Burnham’ s government had the power to take some of the sting out of higher fuel costs, either by extending and increasing the fuel duty cut or reducing VAT, as the government have already done with domestic electricity.

He added:

double quotation mark Without action, 3p a litre in duty will be added on 1 January, and another 2p on 1 March, which will only make prices at the pump even more expensive. At a time when Treasury VAT takings from fuel remain exceptionally high, drivers will be looking to this month’s budget for some much-needed relief.

Former Deutsche Bank trader overtuns rate rigging conviction

The UK’s Court of Appeal has overturned the conviction of Christian Bittar , the Deutsche Bank trader who was jailed for conspiring to rig benchmark interest rates pleaded guilty to conspiracy to defraud.

He was the final trader whose case was being appealed in the UK. Five former Barclays traders had their convictions overturned on Wednesday this week. The cases of seven Libor and Euribor defendants have been overturned in total.

The decision on Bittar’s case comes despite the former trader having pleaded guilty to the charges eight years ago.

Bittar was sentenced to five years and four months in jail, after pleading guilty in 2018 to rigging Euribor, the Euro interbank offered rate that determined the rates on trillions of dollars of financial contracts and loans across the world.

The ruling on Friday further unravels one of the UK Serious Fraud Office’s most high-profile prosecutions.

Jason Williams, head of division at the SFO said in a statement:

double quotation mark We argued for a different outcome but respect the court’s decision in relation to Christian Bittar. The SFO remains committed to tackling the most complex fraud, bribery and corruption.

The European Union is granting temporary trade preferences to Armenia following trade restrictions recently imposed by Russia, our senior correspondent Lisa O’Carroll reports.

In a move which shows how flexible the EU can be, it said the temporary trade preferences “will help alleviate the difficult situation faced by Armenian producers and exporters and support the resilience of Armenia’s economy by facilitating access to the EU market.”

The measures, which will enter into force tomorrow for a period of two years, temporarily allow 80% of Armenian exports to the EU, including almost all exports of fresh fruit, vegetables and flowers affected by the Russian measures, as well as over 91% of exports of beverages and spirits.

Armenia is not an accession state, but has been singled out for support as part of the EU a broader solidarity support package

Data storage firm Snowflake denies Asos breach caused by platform flaw

Data storage firm Snowflake has said hack at Asos was not caused by a vulnerability or flaw with its platform.

It comes after Asos’ investigation this week found an “unauthorised party gained access to an Asos employee account by impersonating a trusted contact to obtain log-in credentials”. Asos said the credentials were then used to access information on third-party platforms used by the company.

But on Friday, Snowflake – a US cloud-based AI data storage business – distanced itself from the incident despite being referenced in the message from the hackers.

(The message had read: “Dear ASOS DPO and IT, we have fully compromised the Snowflake instance. Engage with us, or we will leak it,” followed by a Telegram link.)

A Snowflake spokeswoman said:

double quotation mark We are aware of Asos’s notification to their customers regarding this incident. We can confirm this issue did not in any way result from a vulnerability, weakness, flaw, or misconfiguration with the Snowflake service, platform, or internal environments, and was not caused by Snowflake. No remediation is required for Snowflake customers. We continue to encourage adherence to our security best practices.

Asos has stressed that no payment card information or account passwords were accessed. They added the website and app were safe to use:

double quotation mark There is no action you need to take on your account. However, please remain cautious of unexpected messages or calls claiming to be from Asos. We will never ask you to share passwords, security codes or payment details through an unsolicited message or call.

A quick check in on stock markets:

European stock markets are trading higher, with the FTSE 100 up 0.8%, France’s CAC 40 up 0.77% and Germany’s DAX up 1.07%.

US futures are pointing to a strong start for Wall Street, with Dow futures up 0.17%, S&P futures up 0.4%, Nasdaq up 0.81%.

In London, the FTSE 100 is up despite a 5.4% drop in Airtel Africa shares, which started conditional trading today, as well as a 4.2% drop in Vodafone shares and a 2.3% drop in BT , amid jitters over the prospect that SpaceX could start offering retail telecoms services to US consumers.

Airtel Money shares start trading on London Stock Exchange

Shares in Airtel Money have begun conditional trading on the London Stock Exchange, marking the biggest float in five years.

It is also the fifth biggest company by market value to float on the exchange, excluding those on the international main market.

Shares were priced at £1.96, valuing the company at £5.3bn. (Unconditional trading is expected to start on 14 October.)

Its parent company Airtel Africa – the telecoms provider ultimately controlled by the billionaire Sunil Bharti Mittal – had originally targeted a listing in the first six months of 2026 but delayed it to the second half of the year, blaming unfavourable market conditions as a result of the US-Israeli war on Iran . Several other companies have pushed back planned IPOs amid market volatility.

Airtel Africa was already listed on the FTSE 100, but bosses wanted Airtel Money to be listed separately.

Dan Coatsworth, head of markets at AJ Bell, said it has the potential to encourage more companies to list on the UK stock market:

double quotation mark Chief executives sitting on the fence about whether to choose London as a listing destination might be watching Airtel Money’s success with great interest and noting the decent show of support from retail investors. Airtel Africa’s success will have certainly played a part in Airtel Money also selecting to list in the UK, but so too will the market’s reputation of having a broad range of investors willing to consider companies from any sector and not only being interested in AI-related technology. The UK stock market might have suffered from low tech representation, yet its more diversified interests have shone in recent times when investors have started to question if there is a new tech bubble, and whether it’s about to burst.

Oil prices ease further, Brent crude down 1.3%

Brent crude prices are now down 1.3%, easing further s from where we started – having been down around 1% earlier this morning.

Neil Wilson, an investor strategist at Saxo UK, says Trump’s comments regarding a pause in strikes, have “allayed fears” of a fresh flare-up in the war in the Middle East, following reports that the US was going to resume military action.

double quotation mark Fresh strikes would disrupt the flows that have been painstakingly re-established over recent weeks to pre-war levels, and represents a clear material upside risk to crude prices and term structure. Brent scaled almost $106 before the comments from Trump took it down a couple of bucks to $104 this morning.

OpenAI has revealed that it is making about $20bn less in projected revenue than it had recently indicated to investors, raising questions about the break-neck growth rate in demand for AI.

Th e ChatGPT-maker company has told investors that its revenues for this year would reach $50bn (£37bn), a projection based on sales up to the end of September.

However, this is significantly less than the $70bn that it had signalled in information provided to investors last month, which was widely reported.

Forecasts of annualised revenues by the leading artificial intelligence players, including by OpenAI’s rival Anthropic , the maker of Claude, are closely watched by markets as an indicator of overall demand for a technology that is attracting huge investment.

OpenAI is in early-stage talks to raise $30bn in a funding round that values the business at about $1.4tn.

News of the $20bn gap buffeted US tech stocks on Thursday, with the tech-led Nasdaq closing down by 1.4%. Chip giant Nvidia fell 2.9%, Oracle was down 5.5% and Micron declined 4.8%.

Read more here:

Full story: Donald Trump has promised not to attack Iran before November’s US midterm elections, outlining a pause on the protracted war he has struggled to end after almost eight months.

In a Truth Social post on Thursday, the US president said Washington was “having productive discussions with the Islamic Republic of Iran”, which he claimed was “in very bad condition, both Economically and Militarily”.

The strait of Hormuz, through which roughly a fifth of the world’s oil and liquefied natural gas passed through before the war, was all but closed after the US and Israel struck Iran in late February.

On Thursday, however, Trump suggested that oil was moving through the strait in record volumes: “22 Million Barrels, last night alone”, he claimed, “with not one barrel coming from, or going to, Iran”. The figure could not be independently verified.

“We will not be attacking Iran at any time prior to the Midterm Elections to be held in the United States on November 3rd,” Trump wrote. “IRAN WILL NOT HAVE A NUCLEAR WEAPON!”

Read more here:

It’s worth remembering that this morning’s pullback in oil prices comes after Brent crude posted its biggest daily jump in two weeks, rising more than 4% to $104.28 per barrel.

That was driven by mounting fears of further escalation of the US war on Iran, which this past week was punctuated by Houthi attacks on two attacks in Saudi Arabia , and new attacks on ships in the strait of Hormuz.

US magazine The Atlantic also reported overnight that the White House had asked the Pentagon to develop strike options that could be used before the midterms.

As Deutsche Bank analysts note, “that that ran counter to assumptions that there wouldn’t be an escalation before the midterms.”

UK and US telecom stocks have tumbled after Elon Musk’s SpaceX took a major step towards launching a Starlink mobile service for American consumers.

The company announced it had bought a nationwide low-band spectrum license portfolio that it said would help it launch a full mobile business in the US.

This would be done by providing what it claimed was the world’s “most advanced broadband network from space”:

double quotation mark This prime low-band spectrum addresses one of the key remaining technical gaps that will pave the way for Starlink Mobile to become a major mobile carrier in the US.

The potential competition has spooked investors in some of the US’ biggest mobile carriers. Verizon Communications tumbled 7%, AT&T dropped 7.5% and T-Mobile US fell 6.7%.

Those jitters also weighed on UK telecom stocks, pushing BT (which owns EE) down 0.5% and Vodafone down 2.6% SpaceX currently runs high speed internet connections in more than 160 countries, via its constellations of satellites.

Trump’s pledge to pause attacks on Iran, and China’s resumption of fuel exports, are offsetting concerns about potential disruptions to oil supplies in the US Gulf coast as a result of Hurricane Isaias.

The hurricane, which intensified from a tropical storm into the first hurricane of the 2026 Atlantic hurricane season on Wednesday night, has prompted state of emergency declarations in Florida, Alabama and Georgia.

US producers in the Gulf of Mexico have temporarily halted operations, representing around 1.3 million barrels per day of oil production and 1.1 billion cubic feet per day of natural gas. Reuters reported that personnel had already been evacuated from 121 production platforms, , citing the Marine Minerals Administration. That represents around 33% of the 371 manned platforms in the Gulf, and workers had been removed from five of 11 non-dynamically positioned rigs, it said.

Introduction: Oil prices ease as Trump pledges to pause Iran attacks, and China restarts fuel exports

Good morning, and welcome to our rolling coverage of business, the financial markets and the world economy.

We’re seeing a dip in oil prices this morning, with Brent crude down about 1% at $103 per barrel , following another momentary pause in US attacks on Iran.

Prices eased overnight on news that US president Donald Trump had pledged not to attack Iran ahead of the US midterm elections, which take place on 3 November.

It comes as public support for his war in the Middle East is waning and ultimately weighing on Republican election campaigns.

In a Truth Social post , Trump said:

double quotation mark We are having productive discussions with the Islamic Republic of Iran. I want to make it clear to everybody that, while Iran is in very bad condition, both Economically and Militarily, and while the Blockade will remain in full force and effect, with Oil flowing in Record Numbers of Barrels through the Hormuz Strait (22 Million Barrels, last night alone, with not one barrel coming from, or going to, Iran!), we will not be attacking Iran at any time prior to the Midterm Elections to be held in the United States on November 3rd. IRAN WILL NOT HAVE A NUCLEAR WEAPON!

An Reuters/Ipsos survey from late September show thats only a third of Americans approve of strikes on Iran, while approval for Trump among Republicans had fallen from 82% to 73% in a week.

Polling averages now show Democrats leading Republicans by roughly nine points on the generic congressional ballot, according to forecaster Nate Silver , the widest margin of this election cycle.

Oil prices have also eased on news that China is set ⁠to resume fuel exports, after a pause in deliveries during the country’s Golden Week holiday. The resumption of exports are expected to boost tight global supplies of diesel, gas, and jet fuel.

stories.title: HMV to close Oxford Street store after three years
stories.summary: HMV says it is looking for a new site in London's West End, but its current site is "unviable".

stories.body:
HMV says it is looking for a new site in London's West End

Published 7 hours ago

HMV has said it will shut its flagship Oxford Street store three years after it reopened the site, blaming a proposed doubling of the rent for the closure.

The entertainment chain said it would leave the shop in March 2027, in a move affecting more than 50 staff.

It said it was looking for a new site in London's West End district for its flagship shop and said it planned to maintain a "significant presence" in the capital.

Phil Halliday, managing director of HMV, said it was "frustrating" that the Oxford Street shop was "commercially unviable".

He said: "This is a special store, it's where we began 100 years ago and bringing it back to life in 2023 was a big moment in our recent history.

"We are looking ahead, and our focus is now on what we do to make exciting steps for HMV in 2027."

HMV shut its Oxford Street store in 2019 after it went into administration

The group said its landlords had proposed doubling the rent on the site at 363 Oxford Street, and it was also facing a bill for "substantial" renovation works at the store, which together would make the shop "commercially unsustainable".

HMV said it would look to transfer affected workers to its two other London stores and head office while it looked for a new site.

The chain reopened its historic Oxford Street store in November 2023 after a four-year absence following a deal secured with landlords. It first opened the Oxford Street site in 1921.

HMV has 113 stores across the UK, including six sites under the Fopp brand, as well as another eight in Europe. The group said it remained committed to high street stores.

stories.body:
As The Lucky Son picks up where Cunxin’s 2003 memoir left off, the renowned Chinese Australian ballet dancer reflects on sacrifices made by his wife, his years at a stockbroker, and his success leading the Queensland Ballet

Get our weekend culture and lifestyle email

S ome people live such extraordinary lives that a single autobiography simply won’t suffice. Li Cunxin has now written two. The renowned ballet dancer and former artistic director of Queensland Ballet had hoped he was finished writing his story after the phenomenal international success of his 2003 memoir, Mao’s Last Dancer. But life had other plans.

“Actually, I had signed a contract with Penguin Random House for a follow-up,” Cunxin says, from his home in Brisbane. “It was going to be about the lives of my brothers and friends in China, and the ways the country has changed over time. But then I was offered the job at Queensland Ballet and I had to dedicate all my time to that. I don’t think they were expecting [the sequel] to take 14 years!”

His second memoir, The Lucky Son, takes up precisely where Mao’s Last Dancer left off: as Cunxin and his ballet dancer wife Mary fly to their new lives at Houston Ballet under the directorship of Ben Stevenson. That outline of the proposed book on China can be glimpsed under the surface of this one, like a palimpsest; Cunxin’s six brothers’ lives are sketched, and a fascinating portrait of a country lifting itself from abject poverty to world superpower emerges.

“One of the things my mother taught me was to keep moving forward at all times,” Cunxin says. “Don’t think about the past, just concentrate on what is ahead.” That grit kept her children alive and was instrumental in shaping Cunxin’s dogged, highly ambitious personality.

Determination runs in the family. Mary was a deeply respected dancer herself, a career she sacrificed when she and Cunxin discovered their daughter Sophie was born profoundly deaf. “We were so fearful that Sophie would miss out on so much,” Cunxin says. “Music and dance and all the magical things.”

Mary immediately left the world of ballet (she would return years later as ballet mistress at Queensland Ballet) to teach Sophie to talk. “Mary was incredible,” Cunxin recalls. “She gave everything to the task.”

One one hand, it was a complete success. Sophie was fitted with a bionic ear (then known as a cochlear implant) and thrived; she embraced dance, had a successful education and excelled in the workplace. Cunxin and Mary assumed they’d done all that was needed.

But then in 2015, Sophie sent an email to her parents that shocked and devastated them. Sophie expressed frustration at her parents for wanting their daughter to hear; she felt she’d come halfway to meet their world, but they had not met hers. They had not even bothered to learn sign language. Her “deafness was her birthright”, Cunxin writes in the book. Now, he says, Sophie “is a kind of ambassador between the hearing and deaf communities”. And he and Mary have begun learning Auslan.

Cunxin’s dance career was so exemplary – moving from the Beijing Dance Academy to Houston Ballet, and then to principal artist at Australian Ballet – he could have been forgiven for hanging up his pointe shoes and walking into a lucrative position in a stockbroking firm. Indeed, that’s exactly what he did. An unsuccessful tilt at the artistic directorship of Australian Ballet (the role eventually went to David McAllister) utterly crushed him, and it seemed for a few years he would never return to the world of professional ballet.

Of course, that wasn’t how it panned out: despite being burned by that failure, Cunxin reluctantly put his name in the hat when Queensland Ballet were looking for their next artistic director. That tenacity and resolve was once more poured into the theatre.

“To be a leader of any kind takes vision,” Cunxin says. “I had a very strong vision for Queensland Ballet. But you also have to be a good communicator, because you need to inspire others to join in your vision.” And you need to apply yourself, which wasn’t such an issue for someone trained at Beijing Dance Academy, with its brutal rehearsal regime and exacting standards.

One of the delights of The Lucky Son is the way it tracks some of our favourite characters from Mao’s Last Dancer, including The Bandit, Cunxin’s bestie at the Beijing Dance Academy; his gorgeous instructor Teacher Xiao; and his astonishing mum and dad, Niang and Dia. There are echoes in the events too: Stevenson’s trip to Queensland to watch his protégé mount Cinderella recalls the unforgettable moment in Mao’s Last Dancer when his parents leave China for the first time to see their son dance and the audience gives them a standing ovation.

Central to Cunxin’s success at Queensland Ballet – where he oversaw a massive improvement in standards and built a stunning new home for the company, the Thomas Dixon Centre – were the lessons he learned from his time away from ballet, when he was a stockbroker: “I learned so much from the business world – when we had to approach donors for money, I could speak their language.” Relationships with Elisabeth Murdoch and the Ian Potter Foundation came in handy, and he and Mary also contributed some money of their own. It’s now a world-class organisation.

Looking back on his life now, Cunxin feels an overwhelming sense of “gratitude, for the opportunities I was given and the people and artists who shaped me”. The Lucky Son concludes on stage – hardly surprising, given so many of the key moments in Cunxin’s life have been there – but this time it is in Switzerland, where he was awarded ballet’s most prestigious award, the Prix de Lausanne, in 2025.

After a few years of serious health issues (Mary is a cancer survivor and Cunxin has a major heart condition), the couple are increasingly happy to chill. “Our health has forced us to slow down,” he says with the emphasis on forced, as if there were no way they would slow down on purpose. “I worked very hard for two years on this book – it’s been all-consuming. So yes, I am enjoying taking things a little slower.” Is he confident that ballet will survive the coming AI tsunami, given how hard the art form is to perfect and how much time and effort is required? “I am worried, but I do think ballet is special,” he says. “When people come to see ballet, they are blown away by the artistry, the physicality and the music. I think it’s more important than ever to connect people.”

The Lucky Son by Li Cunxin is out now (Penguin, $36.99)

stories.title: Campaigners claim minister attempting to undermine 'Holiday Hunger Bill'
stories.summary: The education minister has warned it would immediately cost his department £20m a year at a time when it is already struggling to balance its budget.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Paul Givan has now proposed amendments which would give him discretion to decide when the payments would take effect

Published 12 October 2026, 06:23 BST

Campaigners have accused the education minister of attempting to undermine a proposed Stormont law which would help poorer families with the cost of food.

The Democratic Unionist Party's (DUP) Paul Givan has been consistently critical of the legislation which is being brought forward by Sinn Féin assembly member Danny Baker.

Givan has warned it would immediately cost his department £20m a year at a time when it is already struggling to balance its budget.

The Holiday Meals Payment Bill , external would create a new payment for families whose children receive free school meals which would be made during school holidays to help with the cost of food.

'Reservations'

The matter is due to be discussed in the assembly on Monday.

Givan has now proposed amendments which would give him the power to delay implementation.

He will need support from other parties for the amendments to be accepted.

It is not clear if he will get that support, although the Ulster Unionist Party (UUP) has expressed reservations about the proposal.

The payment would be made during school holidays to help with the cost of food

As it is based on school meals, the cost of the scheme would be on the Department of Education.

It is modelled on the School Holiday Food Grant scheme introduced during the pandemic, which paid qualifying families £27 per child every fortnight.

In April, Givan warned MLAs that his department did not have funding for the scheme, so they would be voting to cut education spending if they supported it.

He has now proposed amendments which would give him discretion to decide when the payments would take effect.

A coalition of campaign groups, including the National Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Children (NSPCC) and Save the Children, say the amendments would mean "no guarantees about when, if ever, payments might begin".

They added: "We are calling on all political parties and all MLAs to reject the amendments tabled by the education minister and support the bill as it currently stands."

Baker has said the education minister is attempting to "obstruct" the implementation of the bill.

"His proposals would give him control over when, if ever, holiday hunger payments begin.

"This is an attempt to delay and undermine legislation that has the support of the majority of parties in the assembly."

A Department of Education spokesperson said the minister's amendments "do not seek to delay or block the Bill".

"They reflect the Department's duty to manage its budget responsibly, taking account of financial pressures, competing priorities and the impact of new spending on existing services, particularly at a time when education faces significant financial challenges across the system," they added.

"The amendments fulfil that duty while preserving the Bill's intended purpose. The Bill's key provisions remain unchanged, including eligibility, payment levels, holiday coverage and the Education Authority's responsibilities."

stories.title: How to avoid getting stung if you miss credit card payments
stories.summary: People are increasingly falling behind on credit card repayments, so here's the best way to get debt advice.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Published 12 October 2026, 00:19 BST

An increasing number of people are missing credit card repayments as finances are stretched by rising bills, according to the Bank of England.

Lenders also told the Bank they expected the number of unpaid credit card debts to keep going up this autumn.

This could lead to more demand for advice on how to deal with debts – but, if you are struggling and need help, there are some traps to avoid.

And it is worth remembering that impartial advice is available free of charge from debt charities. So here's what to think about.

How to find help

If you find yourself with money troubles, it can be tempting to seize any opportunity to get things back on track.

Social media and internet search pages are full of supposed quick-fix debt solutions. Cold calls and WhatsApp messages also promise debt help.

But they may well come with upfront fees, unrealistic claims about writing off debt, and pressure to make a quick decision.

Suggestions on the best way to find help include:

Impartial, authorised debt advice comes free. You can find a provider on the government-backed Moneyhelper website , external

Check whether a firm offering debt help is authorised by the regulator, the Financial Conduct Authority (FCA). You should cross-check the authorisation details they give with the FCA's Firm Checker , external

Anyone unhappy with the service from an authorised firm can complain and, if you are still not happy, go to the independent Financial Ombudsman Service.

Alison Walters, director of consumer finance at the FCA, said: "Anyone struggling with debt deserves advice that puts their interests first.

"Free, impartial debt advice is available to everyone, and no one should be pressured or misled into paying for a debt solution that may not be right for them."

The warning signs of being misled

The FCA says that some unregulated firms collect people's details, through cold calling or online adverts, sometimes impersonating debt advice charities or debt collectors, and pass this information on to firms offering debt solutions that you pay for.

A quick search online will throw up lots of businesses offering ways to clear your debt, not all of which are trustworthy, according to charities.

Warning signs of unscrupulous firms include pressure tactics, such as repeated contact, often in messages and on the phone, pushing people to agree to a debt solution, the FCA says.

Some people have been encouraged to change financial details on lenders' paperwork, or are "coached" in ways to respond.

Sometimes people are steered towards a fee-charging debt solution, such as Individual Voluntary Arrangements (IVAs) or some debt management plans, without alternative options being properly explained or offered first.

And, do you know who you are talking to? Ask them who they work for, and check if their details match the firm's official details.

"Before making any decisions around how to deal with your debts, it's always worth getting full, free and impartial debt advice first, exploring all options to clear your debt in the safest and most sustainable way," said Vikki Brownridge, chief executive at debt charity StepChange.
